maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY-STATEMENT AS TO OPEN QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of

Trade and Commerce, not of "political trades and commerce", may I reply to a question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Moose Mountain, when he asked me whether the wheat board will be able to provide an open quota for wheat, oats and barley by the end of the present crop year. I said yesterday in reply to his question that I did not think the wheat board would yet be in a position to answer this question, and I now have an answer from the wheat board.
The exact level of quotas which will be reached by the end of the crop year cannot be determined at the present time. There are two reasons for this. First, the wheat board does not know how much of the grain farmers now hold will actually be delivered. From past experience, as the hon. member knows, this depends a good deal on crop prospects at the time the crop is being delivered. Second, the board does not know the volume of sales, particularly of oats and barley, that will be made between now and the end of the crop year. However, it is known that producers will be able to market more grain this year than last year, and far more than they have delivered on the average in the past ten years.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the amount shown in the main estimates of the Department of Agriculture for the fiscal year 1964-65 is $140,124,800, of which approximately $140 million is to be voted by parliament and $70,000 is authorized by statute.
Included in this total are amounts required for three functions which have been transferred to the Minister of Forestry. These are the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act and the program respecting freight assistance and storage costs on western feed grains. The amounts required for these operations were included in the Department of Agriculture estimates prior to the functions being transferred to the Minister of Forestry. Where functions are transferred pursuant to the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act the appropriations relating to them are treated as appropriations of the department to which they are transferred. Thus while these three items appear in the Department of Agriculture estimates, they will actually be appropriations of the Department of Forestry. The total of these amounts is $31,359,600.
This leaves a balance of $108,695,200 required for the Department of Agriculture for 1964-65. This compares with $105,096,545 for the same functions in the estimates for 196364. I might mention here that this is the gross amount, and it is rather complicated to find out what the net amount is. However, there was something over $13 million on the revenue side which would reduce the $105 million by that amount.
There has been one recent development in connection with departmental operations which I think might be of interest to the committee. This has to do with our research work. We have a very strong and capable research organization within the department. I think the importance of research and its contribution to agriculture are widely understood and much appreciated. It is important, though, that this be brought as closely as possible to the farming community which it is designed to serve. In many of our research stations there is a close and intimate association between the stations and agricultural interests in the area. This, of course, is highly desirable as a means of directing our research work toward matters of primary interest to producers. We are moving to strengthen these contacts.
We made a start in this direction at a meeting which I and officials held in Lethbridge two weeks ago with an advisory committee which I have had set up to advise us

Supply-Agriculture
on the operations of our range experimental station at Manyberries. The committee consists of five prominent ranchers and farmers in southern Alberta. We reviewed our work at Manyberries and received several valuable suggestions from the committee as to the direction that work should take. Both the committee and I and the departmental officers were convinced of the value of this type of arrangement, and we plan to extend it gradually.
The total cash income from the sale of farm products in 1963, $3,220 million, was the largest on record, being 2.2 per cent above the previous record in 1962 of $3,154 million. The net income of farmers in 1963 was $1,716 million as against $1,679 million in 1962. The net income is made up of gross income, including cash income, income in kind and government payments, minus operating expenses and depreciation charges and with an adjustment for inventory changes. Operating expenses and depreciation charges were again higher in 1963, being $2,180 million compared with $2,080 million in 1962. The net income in 1963 was exceeded only in the years 1951 and 1952.
While the net income in 1963 was higher than in 1962, the realized net income was slightly lower at $1,410 million compared with $1,491 million in 1962. The realized net income does not take inventory changes into account. The increase in the inventory value of products on the farm at the end of 1963, compared with 1962, was $307 million.
Another matter which I might mention has to do with agricultural exhibitions. If the exhibitions are to be of the best possible service to agriculture it is important that the classes and prize lists in livestock and other classes be related closely to utility values and encourage widespread participation by breeders. I have had extensive discussions with exhibition people and some of the breed associations about this matter, and I find them very much in accord with our thinking. We are arranging this year at some of the major exhibitions to have some pilot classes as a start toward this objective, and the department will be assisting in the prize money for these exhibitions.
Possibly I should enlarge on exactly what we propose to do with exhibitions, because I am sure hon. members will be interested as will livestock breeders right across Canada. We have some 35 research centres in Canada, along with enough substations to make up a total of 56. There are 128 exhibitions in Canada, and these exhibitions are held in nearly all the important towns or towns of sufficient size to sustain exhibitions.

One group of exhibitions is known as class A because they provide $6,000 or more in prize money for agricultural purposes. Those in class B have to provide $3,000 or more to be eligible for inclusion in class B fairs.
Throughout the years the Canadian government has provided capital grants for these exhibitions to help them to erect buildings of a capital nature to be used for agricultural purposes. These grants were suspended in July of 1962, and for the most part they have not been reinstated. I discussed this matter with the provincial ministers of agriculture last June and again last December, and they were also of the opinion that we should take a whole new look at the exhibition set-up because it does play a very important part in research so far as Canada is concerned. I think we should relate this back to a form of research which we have lost in recent years due to the nature of the animals that are being shown. As I mention the vegetables, fruits and all the commodities that are shown at exhibitions, I will explain our program in relation to them.
This year we thought we would like to tie up this group of people who are the best breeders of livestock in Canada and who provide all the seed stock for our commercial enterprises. I believe they also do a great deal of work in so far as seed is concerned, and I am referring to corn and such things, and all the various activities that take place on the farm in connection with seed.
As a result of our geographical position we have always had a very high cost agricultural economy, but we have a very vigorous group of farmers. I think we have in Canada the best farmers in the world. This is probably a result of our geographical position, because they have to fight against great odds in connection with weather and that sort of thing. When you think of the 12 months pasture they enjoy in the Argentine or the 12 months pasture they enjoy in New Zealand, and when you think that Canada is covered with snow from coast to coast a great deal of the time, you begin to realize the problems the farmers have in competing with other countries of the world.
Concerning exhibitions, we felt we should take a new look at these exhibitions to see if we could not catch up on some of the work upon which our research centres are not moving fast enough. We thought we would tie in this program with the group of farmers raising these high class animals and thus make every exhibition a research centre for the betterment of agriculture in Canada.

We decided to do this first with beef cattle. We chose the Hereford to start with and we hope to extend the program to cover all the things that are exhibited. We chose Herefords because for the most part the breeders of these animals have abandoned exhibitions in Canada. The reason they have abandoned the shows is that fittings are so expensive, the cost of transportation so high and the prize money so small that even if they won all the first awards it was not worth while to exhibit these cattle. These breeders just stayed at home.
We have decided to revise the classifications for Herefords. I can best explain the program by relating it to the one breed and then you will see the direction in which we wish to move. Our breeders readily admit that during the last 10 or 15 years they have not been producing as efficient an animal as is possible. When I say "efficient" I am talking in terms of feed conversion and that sort of thing. It takes about five pounds of grain to make one pound of beef today on the hoof. If you realize that it now requires only two and a half pounds of feed to make one pound of chicken, you will acknowledge the job the chicken people have done in the last few years and you can see the objective that the beef breeders have in Canada.
Even though the production of beef was up this year we thought we would like to make these animals more efficient. We have therefore devised six classes and one steer class instead of the 15 or 20 classes we had before. We will have two classes for yearling bulls. They will have to be born in the spring, at the time when beef cattle should be born, and not in the fall when they are expensive to look after. We say he must be born at this time.
The first class will consist of yearlings at the time of the exhibition; this will give the people of the country an opportunity to see this animal. The next class will be the two year old class. We use this class because this is the time you would purchase a bull if you were going to turn him out and use him as a herd sire. These would be the only two classes you would have as compared with the numerous classes we used to have. We would put all the money on these two classes for bulls.
Then we would have four female classes. We would have the yearling class, and this animal would have to be born in the spring and would be comparable to the animal we would ordinarily slaughter at this time. It would weigh around 1,000 pounds. Then we would take the two year old female, and
Supply-Agriculture
there would be two more classes. There would be a three year old cow with a heifer calf afoot, and the next one must be a cow, three years or over, with a male calf afoot. These would be all the classes we would have in this category.
Then we would have a steer class common to all of these classes. This steer would also have to be born in the spring. Anyone who showed in the herd class would have to show in this steer class. The steer would be shown and then slaughtered. He would be cut in half and half would go into the cooler so people could see him. The other half would be judged on cutability, not on the basis of wholesale cuts so much as getting right down to the hamburg, the steaks and all of the other cuts. He would be judged 50 per cent on the hoof and 50 per cent on cut-ability, in terms of dollars and cents. Suppose, for example, he weighed 1,000 pounds, he would probably yield $271 on the basis of cutability. Another steer of exactly the same weight may bring only $250 on the basis of cutability. As I say, the steer would be judged 50 per cent on the hoof and 50 per cent on the basis of cutability. We would have a weight for it, conversion rates and all this sort of thing.
We feel this is a move in the right direction. I have discussed this with the directors of the Canadian Hereford association, with the directors of A exhibitions and the provincial ministers of agriculture. They all feel it is worth a try. I am happy to start this year with the western fairs, the A circuit. There will be a pilot project in so far as this program is concerned, and the federal government will be contributing half the prize money.
The people concerned with the London exhibition were down here. I feel that around London we have, in so far as Ontario is concerned, some of our very best breeders and some of our very best thinkers They feel we should go one step further and use their exhibition to go ahead with a dairy cattle program. We have suggested that we do away with the young classes and that we start out milkers two, milkers three, milkers four and milkers five. These are the categories that the people from the 30 or 40 different countries who attend these fairs come to this country to buy. In this way we would move toward efficiency in relation to the 128 exhibitions in Canada. It would give us a great deal more research than the people, who are doing a good job, could possibly give us today.

Supp ly-A griculture
In so far as wheat is concerned, we would say that one bushel of wheat must be backed up by 50 acres. We would not be selecting wheat on the basis of making a world wheat king. We would do the same thing with corn and so on through the whole list of items. I thought you might be interested in what we planned by way of getting more and better research in connection with producing seed stock.
In our research station at Manyberries we have 41,000 acres, on which we have 13 projects. I believe the cattle project has been completed for some time. We have also done some work there in crossing Highland cattle. We have selected the five top people around this station, and the people at the station would say, "Well, what do you want us to do; what is needed in this particular area?" This is something whereby the producers will be able to bring their work much closer to the job these research centres are doing. We hope to expand this as soon as we are able to and, as I say, we have 37 of these institutions.
I am sure hon. members will agree with me that when they stop and think of some of the great problems we have or are going to have in agriculture, there is a job which we must do in order to keep up with other countries in the world if our own people are to be able to compete in agricultural products right here in Canada. I mentioned hogs. We have seen our hogs go down in quality while other countries are producing a 10 to 15 per cent more profitable hog on feed conversion. It takes us about 3| lbs, of feed to make a pound of pork. We are speaking now about $4 a pig. I have brought this to the attention of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture which is holding a hog conference in Montreal toward the end of this month, and the members of that organization hope we can work toward getting this job accomplished in a hurry.
I sent a hog mission to Denmark last year and on their return asked them how long it would take to produce a hog to compete with the Danish hog. They replied about 10 years, but at the end of that time the Danes might still be 10 years ahead of us. Therefore we propose to put testing stations right across Canada so we can select these animals that have a feed conversion rate of 2.1 or 2.5 per pound of pork. By doing this we can follow the example we set with our dairy cattle. At one time, out of the 40 recognized world records, Canadian dairy cattle held 38, but today that figure has dropped to about 15.

The Canadian farmer can do this job because he is the best thinking farmer in the world and has proven himself so in many fields. I will give another example of what we can do. Last year we raised about 6 million acres of barley. Most of this barley, particularly in western Canada, was grown for malting purposes, yet only 10 per cent of it was used for malting. Our export markets were down because they wanted a white barley instead of a blue barley, and if the Canadian farmer had grown feed barley we would have had a market for a great deal of it in Japan and possibly China, because it is the sort of barley they want there.
If you stop to think of this 6 million acres of barley and the different varieties, Parkland and Montcalm as compared with Husky and Jubilee, you are talking about 10 bushels to the acre on 6 million acres, which is worth $30 million or $40 million to the farmer. When we speak about hogs of 10 or 15 per cent more efficiency we are speaking about an increase of $35 million, and when we speak of seed wheat we are talking about an increase of 90 million bushels.
If we in Canada do a proper job of research we can produce another $100 or $200 million worth of produce from exactly the same farms and the same land, provided we give the farmers the tools to do the job. To illustrate the kind of job the farmer is doing, in 1936 it took 27 cents of the workingman's dollar to feed his family, while in 1963 it took him only 19 cents. If you take subsidies into account you will find that the Canadian farmer feeds the Canadian workingman, living in an urban district, cheaper than the workingman is fed in any other country in the world. Therefore we have to give the farmers the tools to work with if they are to be the efficient sort of people they can be, producing the finest feed grains, wheat and livestock in the world.
Due to our geographical position we are not plagued with the sort of diseases which tropical countries cannot eradicate. We have high health standards, good farm land and a good group of farmers. But our farmers' image has been tarnished, and I do not know why. The other day I drove into a parking lot in Ottawa where a chap asked me "Are you from western Canada"? When I told him I was he asked, "How do you like all that money we send you to keep you on your farm"? We have to change this attitude. It is not helpful. When you stop and think about the amount of money we use from our budget on agriculture it is not much more than the C.B.C. uses. We know we like culture and

that sort of thing, but you cannot watch it with an empty stomach.

My first word, Mr. Chairman, must be of congratulation to the minister. I do not think anyone can deny the tremendous interest that he aroused on this side of the chamber, and I hope on his own side, with his views on research and bringing research closer to the people. Having made that observation I would like to go on and, if I may, preach a political moral.
One of the chief responsibilities of a minister is to try to see the whole picture. I can illustrate this not only by the old story of not being able to see the forest for the trees but also by a much more cogent political anecdote. Once a very experienced politician was talking to a group of new politicians and he wanted to assess their political judgment. He asked them, "If you were put into a closed field and in that field there was a wild bull and a wild bear, and you had a rifle with one round of ammunition, which animal would you shoot"? Of course the bright politician came back with the answer "I would shoot the bear. A politician can always shoot the bull."
I tell this story to illustrate my theme. What we heard this morning was a very fine statement on how we should use our research institutions to carry the knowledge and know how of our scientists right down on to the farms. This is very important, and I agree with the minister that it is long overdue. Each one of us who has gone through the farm areas of the country has seen some farmers using all the knowledge of the technician and the scientist and doing very well, but in the very same areas other farmers are not using the knowledge which is available. This is something to challenge any minister of agriculture, and the minister should be complimented for taking on this task.
Now I have to go on and say that I hope, in chopping away at this tree in the forest, he does not forget the over-all picture because from the statements that have been made by the minister and others in the last year one begins to wonder if in the Liberal government there is this over-all comprehension of the basic and fundamental needs of agriculture. Once or twice during his speech today the minister indicated that he had a little glimmer of what these needs were.
There has been a tremendous concentration by the Department of Agriculture on the techniques of increasing production, making two seeds grow where one grew before, putting more pounds of beef on cattle, on poultry
Sup p ly-A griculture
meat and hog meat, side by side with a lower grain input. What has been missing over the long years of the department's history has been the concept that it is of no use getting farmers to produce things and then leading them into a blind alley because there are no markets at the end of the road. The minister should be praised for grappling with this problem of lack of contact between the work done in the scientific and technical fields of his department and the farmers in general. He realizes that this knowledge has to get to the farmer, and I think he should be congratulated for the remarks he has made today. This is not the end of course, and a great deal remains to be done, but the hon. gentleman will find us ready to support him in the efforts he is making in this direction, as the applause he heard at the end of this part of his observations indicates.
This is not to say the minister should lose sight of the whole picture. I have been collecting the hon. gentleman's speeches made over the past few months, and some of them do indicate that he realizes the nature of the problems which are facing us. I should like to remind the hon. gentleman of what he said last October-it was on October 14-speaking on a supply motion, and again speaking on the estimates on December 12. In his speeches since then he has indicated also that there are three legislative acts which he wishes to bring forward. One has something to do with crop re-insurance. We have heard this since last October, and speeches touching on it were made on March 18 out in Regina intimating that these measures were ready. Then the minister went on to make a statement about two weeks ago to the effect that he was being delayed, that these things were being held up and that he could not get his proposed legislation on the order paper.

I should like to correct one statement. I did not say I could not get it on the order paper. That is not correct. I said the house was so slow in getting legislation through that we lacked time to deal with some of these very important measures. I did not say we had trouble in getting it on the order paper.

Of course we shall accept the minister's word for it. I know the difficulty we have at times. But I wish he would consult the Lethbridge Herald and ask the editor to correct the absolute nonsense which was printed on that occasion. Here is an editorial from the Lethbridge Herald dated April 11 and entitled "The Farmers Wait".
The need for new parliamentary rules has been graphically illustrated by remarks of Canada's

Minister of Agriculture, Hon. Harry Hays, during his recent visit to Lethbridge.
He has three important measures waiting to be brought before the House of Commons, but he can't get them there. The government's legislative program is bogged down by an opposition filibuster, and under the present rules nothing can be done about it except invoke closure. And the Liberal party is still licking its wounds from the last time, eight years ago, that it tried that.
Would the hon. gentleman please write to the editor of the Lethbridge Herald telling him to take out this arrant nonsense and that the minister can, at any time he wishes, put something on the order paper so we would at least know there was something tangible ready. We would give it first reading so we could consider it. We would look at it. I think the statement to which I have just referred is one which should be corrected. If the minister has this legislation ready he should put it on the order paper-
Providing there is something to put there.
-and not go around letting innocent editors think this house is holding up any legislation for agriculture.
Oh, oh.

The next point I should like to make has to do with the cost of farm machinery, a question about which we have heard a great deal. I have the experience of an investigation which was carried out in Saskatchewan over the years, and I have participated in investigations which took place here in Ottawa. As a matter of record, an investigation into the cost of farm machinery was being carried on by the standing committee on agriculture and colonization at the time the government changed. I understand that the present standing committee on agriculture and colonization has so far only held an organization meeting and, if my information is correct, nothing has been referred to it.
Here we have an incomplete study of the cost of farm machinery carried out in the 1962-63 session. Also, up to the end of the last session the same standing committee was working on a major item of cost to eastern farmers, that is the cost of eastern feed grain. We had brought in all these witnesses to give evidence. The committee, composed of Liberals, Conservatives and representatives of the Social Credit group, the Creditistes and the New Democratic party, were all working closely together to try to find effective ways of reducing the cost of eastern feed grain. I suggest to the minister that rather than going out to the west and saying that the opposi-

tion is delaying these things, we should make use of the machinery which is available in parliament under the present rules. Some of the most able men in this country would be glad to sit on this committee, to forget party differences and see whether they could not get at the factors responsible for this situation in which feed grain represents the major item of cost to eastern farmers.
I was hoping to hear from the minister an indication that agriculture is confronted with other problems in addition to the one respecting research. The biggest item of cost to eastern farmers is the cost of feed grain. In this regard the minister seems content with the action he took last summer, hoping that this will achieve the results he desires in stabilizing the price of grain to eastern farmers. At that time I indicated we had grave doubts that the action taken by the minister would get to the root of the trouble, and if hon. members would read the findings of the standing committee I think they would agree that my observations were well founded. So my proposal today is that the minister get on with his work to trying to bring the research done in the department closer to the people, but that he should not neglect these other aspects to which I have referred.
I hope he will look at another tree in the forest. Eastern farmers find themselves in most desperate need. I put on record last October that farm income had moved upward in the western provinces and that it was holding fairly steady in Ontario, but the rise in Ontario was held down by the fact that many of the areas were not as productive as they should be. In Quebec and the maritimes, however, we were facing one of the greatest challenges in the whole field of agriculture.
During the last election campaign-the last two, as a matter of fact-I asked the Conservative party to back me in a program concentrated on raising the farm income of eastern farmers, and by "eastern farmers" I have always meant to include those of British Columbia. I was opposed by the western Liberals, one of whom was elected to the legislature in Regina the other day, on the ground that I was going out to help eastern farmers and should be defeated. I carried this campaign into every constituency in the west and the western farmers supported me; they supported this program of having the federal government concentrate its interest for a few years on lifting up the eastern farmers as we have done in the west. We did not do anything against

the eastern farmer as a government. Indeed, our policy of finding world markets for western grain not only led to an immediate rise in income of western farmers but also caused an updraft which was of benefit to eastern farmers.
This was not enough. There had to be concentrated planning on several of their problems, and I outlined a six point program to meet those problems. We have been waiting for a long time to see what government policy would be.
During the election campaign the national Liberal program was first of all to get at this problem by naming two ministers of agriculture and thus raising the importance to agriculture of the departments of the two ministers. Since that time what have they done? They have decimated the department and made it look like a skeleton; and you know, Mr. Chairman, what a skeleton looks like out on the open street. They have taken the Department of Agriculture, and instead of being one of the two or three top departments of the government they have put it down to No. 20 or No. 23 on the list. First of all they took away the wheat board, which was the marketing arm of the department, and emasculated the whole idea of bringing agriculture into a co-ordinated and cohesive policy making machine.
No sooner had they done that-and we had a second minister of agriculture sitting in the wings for almost a year-then they began to cut the department to shreds and scatter it all over the place. I am not opposed to the moving of any sections of a department if greater good can be accomplished, but I think what has actually happened is that the Department of Agriculture has now become diversified.
During the course of his estimates I should like to ask the minister to answer some questions as to what these statements which have been made recently mean. I have not had much chance to go over what has been happening in Canada recently. For example, this is a headline in the Manitoba Co-Operator of April 2, 1964:
Sauve says new department independent.
The federal government's proposed new department of forestry and rural development is going to operate as an independent unit free of agriculture department controls-
Now, Mr. Chairman, this is not the way to get at our agricultural industry. We have been working for years to bring to agriculture all possible uses of the land which we have such as forestry, for recreation, for any use whatsoever which will increase the income of
Supply-Agriculture
farmers on that land, as one of the techniques of trying to lift the incomes of farmers on marginal land. Yet we now have a minister saying in a farming paper that this new department is going to be independent, and that is what I am concerned about.
Here we have a government trumpeting that they are centralizing the military services after many years of discussion to get efficiency, co-ordination and cohesion into the military operations in this country, yet at the same time the government are diversifying agriculture. Who is going to finance the military if the farmers are not in good shape? Agriculture is still the basic force for building up the economy of the whole country, and when agriculture is doing well every workingman in the cities of Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Hamilton, Montreal and all across the industrial country does well. If you ever reverse the tide with regard to agriculture, then in two or three years you will find the workingman out of work again.
Yet we have agriculture, which we fought like anything to get moving again, all of a sudden being divided up.
There have been words spoken about two or three ministers working together; the Minister of Trade and Commerce looking after wheat, the Minister of Forestry looking after redevelopment and the Minister of Agriculture looking after railway line abandonment, and out of this triumvirate we would get a co-ordinated policy. When I was minister of northern affairs and national resources and responsible under the laws of this country for the planning of all the uses of resources of the country, both in co-operation with other departments of the federal government and with provincial governments and private business, we were working out plans for agricultural redevelopment and plans for the Department of Forestry.
At that time I made no secret, either privately or publicly, of the fact that the job of the minister of northern affairs and national resources was simply planning the operations, but that the Department of Agriculture would be the operating arm because they had the tremendous experience and ability in their department and the staff to co-ordinate the work of all these departments in order to bring the help of all the experts in forestry, recreation, wildlife and all the rest of it to bear on bringing more income to the land. But in the planning which we carried out in our national development program and in its component part, the national agricultural program, the agriculture department was looked on as the heart and muscles

Supply-Agriculture
for the carrying out of the programs worked out by the various departments concentrating on the problem in their particular segments, because in that agriculture department we had the machinery. This government has reversed the whole thinking of the previous national agricultural program, and the test is going to be whether this diversification of a once great department and its relegation down to a subsidiary position in the over-all scale of things in the new regime will lift up farm incomes.
I am going to suggest to the minister in all seriousness that the real challenge before any agriculture minister today must be not just the individual problems of agriculture but that of seeing the situation as a whole. I will let him tell us what he is going to do about his program for cutting down the cost of farm machinery, about his crop reinsurance program and the changes in the Farm Credit Corporation; and we are sitting here ready and willing to help that legislation through the house if there is going to be anything in it to help agriculture. Therefore we would ask for a statement from the minister in this regard.
Now, basically these are the big problems. The big problems in Canada are traced by the research into the income which comes to the farmer. The minister mentioned that in 1963, which was one of the greatest years in the agricultural history of the country, the net income of the farmer was slightly higher. Gross income was up 2 per cent. He went on to confess that costs had also gone up, and then he mentioned the key matter, that the realized net income was down.
Mr. Chairman, the farmer does not give a hoot for any net income figures, and I hope that the minister throws those out of his lexicon. All these net income figures represent bookkeeper's figures. Whenever a farmer grows a big crop the bookkeeper adds the inventory on to his income, but he does not get any cash. Then when he sells his big crop the inventory value is taken off his net income they say his pockets are full. So that net income is meaningless. What one should look at is realized income. The minister said this was down in 1963. It certainly was not down in western Canada in 1963. Therefore it must have been down in eastern Canada.
This is the problem, Mr. Chairman. You have one segment of the industry going up much faster than another sector, so that any program which does not concentrate on the needs of the eastern farmers today is missing the main target. On the minister's estimates

last year I asked him, where is this national dairy policy? We had been grappling with that over the last two years of our term of office and had finally got the industry to sit down with us at a conference in February, 1963, where the late Dr. Hannam made his last great effort. He was chairman of the conference.
Last October I asked what was being done. We did get an announcement about a year ago, just before May 1, relating to price supports. We are still waiting for the price supports for this year even though May 1 is very close. As I pointed out last year in my statement on the estimates, price supports are only a short term policy for one year. What the dairy farmers are concerned with, as well as the great bulk of the dairy industry in eastern Canada, is when we are going to get a national dairy policy. These farmers knew that we were working on it and that it was a very difficult matter. They knew that we had to get co-operation from the provincial governments. We got that co-operation from Quebec and Ontario, and they knew that the others would follow. But what has this government done to grapple with the long range problem of the dairy industry?
We do not know yet.

No, we do not know. I suggest that is what we want to hear about. What has happened to the income of the eastern farmers? The minister skipped over that point when he said it is down for the whole of Canada; but since it was up for the west last year it must be down for the east. We want to know what he is going to do with this legislation; but above all we want to know what is going to happen with regard to a national dairy policy. That is the greatest blistering sore on the whole agricultural industry today. I know the problem is tough and it will be difficult to get the co-operation of the provinces and the farm organizations.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Is it not true that this is a record year for the dairy farmers, and that they have received more in Quebec than they have ever received since confederation?

I am very glad the minister asked that question, Mr. Chairman, because it makes me despair of any hope for him in the future. It is no use worshipping these little figures that are published and show an increase of a percentage point. I will let some

of the members from Quebec answer that question in detail. It is no good taking comfort from an increase of a percentage point; you cannot get away from the basic fact that the minister is pinning all his faith on the hope that the present system will work its way out of the difficulties. I am pointing out to the minister something I am sure is right; that unless there is radical action in connection with the dairy industry, they will never be out of trouble. Because cheese, or some other product, is up a percentage point the minister says "We will get out of the trouble"; but he will not get out of the trouble, because the trouble is fundamental.
Mr. Chairman, could I ask the hon. member a question?

I should like to finish my remarks, Mr. Chairman. The minister will have to face up to the fact that the dairy industry is now national and is not centered around some city. The products are marketed all across the country, and the problems are exactly the same in the United States and 20 or more countries in Europe. Unless this question is faced in a national way in order to get at the basic, fundamental problems involved, the minister will not find a solution.
I suggest that the first fundamental is marketing. We will not be able to market these products in countries where there is a surplus of dairy products. Going over the GATT conferences and spending all your time talking about what you are going to do, and trying to sell dairy products to countries which have a surplus of such products is like milking a dried-out cow. That is what the minister is doing.
The minister must get at the fundamentals of the dairy program; he must work with the farm organizations, bring them together and get the support of the provincial governments. I know that the minister of agriculture of Quebec and the minister of agriculture of Ontario are willing to work together, but there is no leadership from Ottawa. We waited to hear something about that today, but we did not. Did the minister have a question?
No.
He forgot.
Yes, he forgot. I think I have said enough, Mr. Chairman, to make my point. In going after the individual trees in the forest-

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question? Why didn't he do more about it?
Supply-Agriculture

Mr. Chairman, I think this indicates the bankruptcy of policy or ideas of the minister. After holding office for a year, with the most pressing problem facing agriculture as a whole, that of the dairy industry, he asks what could we do about it. I know that when I was in the department there were at least 15 different alternatives, and at least one or two showed signs of promise. We pulled in representatives of farm organizations and set up a committee. How many times has that committee met? What leadership has been given by the minister? He has available in the department all these alternatives, but the real task is to get down and choose the alternative that in his judgment is best and try to take some action on it. It will not be done quickly, but he will have a great deal of co-operation from the minister of agriculture in Quebec and the minister of agriculture in Ontario.
He cannot get any from his colleagues, though.

That is right. I have made my points as well as I can, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the tremendous challenge of the declining farm income in eastern Canada. I like to think that the two hon. members from rural Quebec who came over to support us did so because they came to this house as a protest against the poor agricultural conditions in their part of the country, and the government has done nothing about this.
Hear, hear.

They have heard the debates in this house. They heard the debate during the supply motion last October, in which I indicated in statistical form the sliding income of Quebec and the maritimes in particular. I suggested several directions in which the government could go. Then they heard the minister's answer, that statistics are for losers and that all this was a pile of junk. I do not think it is a pile of junk to put before the house statistics which indicate that there is a pressing problem in certain parts of Canada.
Last December during my remarks on the estimates I asked the minister whether he had knowledge of the farm survey we conducted in 22 districts of eastern Canada in January, 1963. I said at that time that I would not ask him to produce the document, because much of that document is shocking in its significance and if the rest of the people of Canada found out just how poor were the farmers and how low was their standard of living in a great part of our farm population,

Supp ly-A gricu Iture mostly in northern and eastern Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes, there would be a demand on any government, Conservative or Liberal, to take action; because we cannot let 25 per cent of our people live in what can only be described, in city parlance, as slum conditions.
This problem is not new. With regard to this survey, I am coming to the conclusion, since I cannot get the government to take any action in regard to it, that we should ask the minister to publish it and let the people of Canada see what it is like to live in certain counties not very far from here, and counties through Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. We did not even make a survey of Newfoundland because we knew what it was like without making a survey. We should let the people of Canada see just how their fellow Canadians live in this country. Let that survey be published and let us begin to draw the conclusions that must be drawn from the survey and take action against these problems.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired, unless he has unanimous consent to continue.
Agreed.
I am quite content, Mr. Chairman, to stay within my limit of 30 minutes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member please continue. He has unanimous consent.

I have just about finished my remarks anyway. I say with all the force at my command that all parties in this house will stand behind the minister in any courses of action which are constructive and which move forward. I think the two basic problems are, first, the dairy industry-which is a national problem but is mostly concentrated in the east-and second the low income of eastern farmers. We from the west, with almost every seat represented by Conservatives at the present time, will stand behind the minister in any program that will help lift up our fellow Canadians.
That may be more support than he has from the Liberal party.

If I may impose on the committee for a moment or two longer, Mr. Chairman, I have in my hand a whole mass of promises made by the Prime Minister. I do not want to take up too much time, but I will quote just a few:


A new Liberal government will take the initiative in formulating, in co-operation with the provinces, with farmers and milk distributors, a system of free milk for children in school.
This will only help the dairy industry to the extent of 1 per cent, but it is a little help and we will support it. Then with respect to dairy cattle the Prime Minister said this:
With respect to dairy cattle, the objectives will be to have at least 25 per cent of dairy cows on test within ten years.
I do not know how much the candidate concerned knew about the dairy cattle industry, but I would like to know what is happening with regard to these matters. Then the Prime Minister spoke about eastern agriculture, about which nothing has been done to solve the problems. He said:
Under no circumstances will a new Liberal government allow the Crowsnest rates to be eroded or abandoned by any branch line abandonment policy.
Well, they put the minister in charge of branch line abandonment, and he would not tell us what the policy was before the Saskatchewan election, so I do not think it bodes too well for us in this regard:
Would immediately provide for a floor price of $2 a bushel for No. 1 northern wheat and appropriate differentials for other grades to apply over the life of the present international wheat agreement.
Here is another promise in respect of a two price system for wheat:
This policy will be accompanied by a consumer subsidy so that there will be no rise in the price of bread.
Bread has gone up in price but there is no consumer subsidy. Here is another statement made in Regina by the Prime Minister:
Tonight X pledge that we will move immediately to increase the funds available under the Export Credits Insurance Act for financing farm exports.
I have not heard a peep about amending the Export Credits Insurance Act. I can go right through this whole long list, page after page of such promises. Here is another one:
A Liberal government will promptly seek agreement with the provinces on a plan which will enable marketing boards to operate on a national scale-
What is happening there? And so on. I am not suggesting that all these things outlined by the Prime Minister are going to be done. He has gone 60 days in one direction and then 300 days in the other direction. He now says there is a change in policy. He goes one way for 60 days and another way for the other 300 days. All this confusion is bad enough in the case of other ministers who are

new at their jobs and do not know much about Canada, but the Minister of Agriculture has, I am sure, the solid support of every member of every party for any move that will help agriculture. We know that the problems are difficult but I say to him now, bring in the legislation. Put some evidence before us that you have a national dairy policy. Bring some evidence before us that you really want to tackle the problem of the low income of eastern farmers. If you do these things you will get our support.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I see the Minister of Justice rising at the same time as the hon. member for Vancouver East. It has been the custom on the first item to have a statement of policy or in any event a general statement from a representative of each party. I suggest that we should follow the same procedure; therefore I call on the hon. member for Vancouver East.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether an electrician can throw any light on agricultural policies, but I should like to make an approach to agricultural problems without going into details with regard to the various phases of the agricultural economy.
I was most interested in the remarks of the previous speaker. Time after time he spoke about the need to get down to fundamentals. Time after time he spoke about the need for a national agricultural policy. I do not know of any man or woman who stands for election in Canada or who has been elected to any of the legislative chambers of Canada who would not make exactly the same kind of statement, the same kind of speech and utter the same kind of platitudes and generalities. Platitudes and generalities are not the important thing. The important thing is, when is somebody going to have the courage to tell governments and agriculturists that they have got to face up to the problem and perhaps accept things that go against their grain?
We are not going to solve the problems of agriculture with policies based on bits and pieces. We have got to get down to the groundwork of doing the thinking for a national agricultural policy that will cover all phases of agriculture and will tie in agriculture from the west to the east, from the Pacific to the Atlantic. If we are going to approach the major problems of agriculture in that manner then government members, official opposition members and others are going to have to face up to an analysis of the Canadian economy and the principles that govern that economy.
Supply-Agriculture
We have heard a great deal said about the fact that in Canada we live under a private enterprise system and are proud of it. But, Mr. Chairman, you cannot separate the agricultural economy from the over-all economy, and if you honestly analyse our over-all economy today you will see that so far as the federal authority is concerned, we are rapidly getting away from a free enterprise system to a subsidized economy system.
Let us face the facts. So far as the federal government is concerned it is already subsidizing many aspects of the over-all economy. We subsidize the gold mines, we subsidize the coal mines; we subsidize the railways; we subsidize the shipping industry.
The manufacturers, through the tariff.

Through tariff procedures we subsidize the vast majority of manufacturers in Canada. We have a subsidized economy not only generally but in agriculture as well. May I make it very clear that in the 11 years I have been a member of the House of Commons I have always supported agricultural subsidies because of need and emergency, but we have passed the stage where such subsidies are granted only for a year, three years or five years. They have now become a part of the agricultural economy, a part of the subsidized economy of Canada, and we are not going to get down to a basic understanding of the problems and how to meet them unless we face that fact.
Just before I call it one o'clock I should like to say something so that it will appear in this portion of my remarks. If Canada does not have a secure agricultural economy, with those engaged in agriculture receiving incomes comparable with the incomes of other workers, this country is in trouble. If agriculture fails we do not eat, and if we do not eat we die. This is fundamental and basic, so let us start with this premise.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speechtext:
When we adjourned for lunch at one o'clock the hon. member for Vancouver East had the floor. I understand the Minister of Justice has a short contribution to make to the debate and, since he has another obligation later this afternoon it has been suggested that he be allowed to make his contribution now and the hon. member
