for Vancouver East would reserve his right to continue and terminate his speech later. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I first thank the hon. member for Vancouver East for his co-operation in agreeing to suspend his interesting speech to allow me to fulfil an undertaking which I had given to the house on March 31 last. At that time, at the request of the Minister of Transport, I told the house I would, along with my officers, analyse the events which took place between February 3 and February 20, 1964, that is between the time the first order in council was passed, which purported to transfer from the Minister of Agriculture to the Minister of Forestry certain of the powers of the Minister of Agriculture, and another order in council of February 20 by which the first order in council was annulled and rescinded. I could have limited myself to making a statement on motions, but in view of the opinions which I have given to the cabinet on all the facts involved, I thought it would be fairer to the members of the house if I made a statement in committee, thereby enabling hon. members to question me on any aspect of the statement.
I wish to inform the committee of several actions taken by the government in response to certain questions raised when the transfer of duties between the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Forestry was discussed in committee of supply. In the debate that took place in committee of supply on this matter, following the statement of the Minister of Transport on March 26, hon. members opposite raised certain questions and it is important that these be dealt with. First of all, there is clearly some uncertainty in the minds of some hon. members concerning the actual effect of the three orders in council, No. 157 of February 3, 1964; No. 295 of February 20, 1964 and No. 360 of March 5, 1964. Questions were raised about the status of actions which may have been taken by or in the name of the ministers concerned, particularly during the period between the first two orders.
The committee will recall that on March 31 I undertook to have the officers of my department look at the actions in the period between February 3 and February 20 which might have been affected by the orders in question. This has been done, and a copy of a letter addressed by me to the Prime Minister on April 20, which reports my findings, has now been tabled. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that under
[The Chairman.]
the rules of this house, even as Minister of Justice, I am not entitled formally to give an opinion to the house. However, since I am the legal adviser to the crown and the cabinet, to all the ministers, I thought the way to obviate the difficulty would be for me to advise the cabinet by way of letter, which I have to do anyway, signed by me under my own responsibility. This letter has been tabled by way of a report to the house as to what I may have advised the cabinet. This may be a little technical, but I think it puts my position properly in relation to the constitution and will enable me to answer questions put by hon. gentlemen.
As is suggested in that letter, an order in council has been passed in the interim to remove any uncertainty that might still exist. The number of this order in council is P.C. 1964/600, dated April 23, and it has already been tabled. I would draw the attention of the committee to three particular aspects of it. First of all, the order recites that certain powers, duties or functions which had, by an order of February 3, been transferred from the Minister of Agriculture to the Minister of Forestry were retransferred to the Minister of Agriculture by the order of February 20. The effect of these words is to remove any possible doubt about what is referred to by the Leader of the Opposition as the effect of that second order.
Second, the last paragraph of the order of April 23 confirms all things done since February 3 by or in the name of the two ministers concerned under the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, the Farm Credit Act, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
Third, the new order makes one slight addition to the provisions of P.C. 1964/360 of March 5, relating to the administration of the programs respecting freight assistance and grain storage costs on western feed grains. Unlike the other matters transferred to the Minister of Forestry, these programs have no specific legislative basis other than items in annual appropriation acts.
Words have therefore been added to make it clear that the transfer of these powers, functions and duties is to have continuing effect in the new fiscal year and future years as the programs are extended by subsequent appropriation acts.
While there appears to be no legal necessity whatever, we will make assurance doubly sure by having the eight ARDA agreements, signed by the Minister of Agriculture during

the period February 3 to February 20, reexecuted by the Minister of Forestry.
The second principal aspect of this matter which was called into question in committee of supply concerned publication. We have considered very carefully the arguments presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and we have done two things. First, we have decided that in the future copies of all orders passed under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer Duties Act will be tabled. As an earnest of this decision I have today tabled a copy of an order, P.C. 477, passed on April 6 for the transfer to the departments of public works, transport, and northern affairs and national resources of the principal responsibilities of the Department of National Defence relating to Fort Churchill.
There remains the question whether or not orders passed under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act require publication under the terms of the Regulations Act. This, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will be the first to recognize, is not a question of policy but of legal interpretation. The practice in the past was, I think, clearly stated by the Minister of Transport on March 26, and it will be seen from my letter that I am of the opinion that such orders are of an administrative character and not an exercise of a legislative power. However, we share the view of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre as to the public interest in these orders.
I am authorized by the Prime Minister to state that henceforth, so long as this government is in office, we will alter the previous practice. Any orders made under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act will be published in the Canada Gazette. They will also, as I have already said, be tabled in the house, and they will therefore have in substance the treatment they would be required to have if they were regulations within the meaning of the Regulations Act.
I think that points raised by hon. gentlemen opposite, on the occasion of the discussion of these particular estimates, in relation to the effect of the two first orders in council and with respect to the possible application of the publication provision in the Regulations Act, have had the advantage of making the government reconsider a practice which, in my opinion, was a valid one, and at the same time has enabled the government to modify that practice so that in the future these orders in council, which are of interest to the public, will henceforth be
Supply-Agriculture
published and brought more directly to the knowledge of all members of the public.

On this point, before the hon. member for Vancouver East continues his speech, I would like to say we are glad that the minister and the government have agreed henceforth to table these orders in council. This will be of great assistance to hon. members and the people of the country.
Did I understand the minister to say that an order in council of April 23 has validated any agreements that were signed by the Minister of Agriculture and they will now be considered to have been signed by the Minister of Forestry?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There is, if the hon. member allows me to so state, a slight distinction to be made. As I said, they have been confirmed, which I think is different from being validated. This is my opinion, and I have advised the government very specifically in this matter. I have tried to place myself back 13 months ago, when I was practising law on Dorchester street in Montreal and advising a client in the most practical possible fashion. It is my opinion, and I have so advised the government, that the effect of the order in council has not been to invalidate any of the administrative acts which had been passed in the interval, but in order to avoid any doubt henceforth, the order in council of April 23 purports to confirm, that is to sanction and recognize, whatever has been done.
The principle that we have invoked and applied is that of agency. There is no doubt that the minister, on the occasion of a rearrangement of powers or a transfer of powers, becomes the agent of the government to that extent, and it is always the power of a principal to confirm whatever has been done in an imprecise period by an agent. But this has been done exclusively as a precautionary measure, and so as to make sure in the public interest that none of these acts may be brought into question at any time.
But I have this to say at the present moment. There are two types of acts which have been performed by the ministers concerned in the interval, or rather by the employees or officers of the two departments, and these are administrative acts. The acts of pure administration have been performed by the employees of the crown in their respective capacities in the name of the crown, and I am quite sure that each of them has purported to effect these acts in his respective capacity. So long as they were acts of pure

Supply-Agriculture
administration they were done on behalf of the crown, and they are not to be put into question.
But there were two types of acts with respects to which I must admit that some doubts have been raised in my mind. The first of these concerns the signing by the Minister of Agriculture of eight agreements with the provinces under ARDA between February 3 and February 20-around February 10 or February 15. So far as those are concerned, it is my view that the cancellation of the order in council of February 3 by the order in council of February 20 has had the effect of restoring the complete application of these statutes which vest these powers with the Minister of Agriculture. But for the sake of more precaution I have advised that the minister charged with the administration of ARDA should now sign these agreements so as to eliminate any possible doubt. On February 10, I believe it was, the minister appointed one person to act in connection with a program, jurisdiction over which had been transferred to the Minister of Forestry. There was doubt in my mind that he was entitled to make the appointment at that time, but the appointment was reconfirmed after February 20, that is after the order rescinding the first one had been made. So now there is no doubt that the reappointment now by the Minister of Agriculture was validly made.
One other question may arise and it concerns the validity of the acts performed by that appointed official between February 10 and February 20. I have not checked as to the number of functions performed but it is my opinion, as appears from the letter I have sent to the Prime Minister, that the application of the doctrine which is well known in law and which is called the de facto doctrine has the effect of confirming those acts. This doctrine means that when a person is appointed to discharge certain public functions, a judicial function, for instance if say, for certain technical reasons, the appointment was invalid, so long as the person concerned purported to perform acts which would normally have been within his jurisdiction, then he acted de facto as the person who might otherwise have carried out such acts, and from the standpoint of the public those acts are confirmed. There are a number of decisions in the case of minor judicial appointments cases where the original appointment has been declared to be invalid but where the decisions rendered by the person holding the office have been declared to be valid. Why should this be so? It is because

the public may not suffer as a result of the invalidity of an appointment so long as the person appointed purported to carry out duties which would normally come within the jurisdiction he would have acquired had he been validly appointed. Anyhow, it is my view that the order in council of April 23 has the effect of removing all doubts as to the validity of what was done previously.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question? Would he say with regard to the order in council of April 23 whether this order in council in fact indicates that an error or a breach of the law was committed in the month of February?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No. It is the case that a legal adviser, whether he be the Minister of Justice or anyone else is not only entitled to his own view, but has the responsibility of forming one. On the other hand, no single legal adviser in a situation like this one which is, to a certain extent, complex, can be conceited enough to believe definitely that there is no possible doubt as to the complete validity of what has been done. We have wonderful judges in the superior court, but there are occasions when their judgments have to be reconsidered by the court of appeal. Even in the supreme court one may find four judges holding one view on a point of law and the other holding a different view. So my conclusion was that in the public interest, for the purpose of better continuity of the administration of the affairs of Canada, a way should be found of removing all doubt as to what has been done in the past, and confirming whatever has been done in case there may be some question as to its validity.
I think it is the obligation of the government to pass whatever measures are likely to achieve such a purpose. The opinion I gave to the Prime Minister represents my opinion in accordance with my full responsibility as Minister of Justice, and my recommendation for the passing of the additional order in council and for the re-execution of the ARDA agreement is one which ought not to be interpreted as a declaration of the invalidity of or in condemnation of what was done in the past. Rather, it was a recommendation made in accordance with my responsibility as a minister of the crown, so that a double measure of assurance might be given to the people of this country.

It seems to me that the minister is being very gentle when he says the order in council of April 23 was merely to

confirm those eight agreements with the provinces, rather than to validate them. It seems to me that from February 3 until February 20 the right to sign those agreements was not in abeyance-it had been vested in the Minister of Forestry under order in council 157 which was passed on February 3. It seems perfectly plain that the Minister of Agriculture had no legal authority at all to sign those orders. So to say that the order in council of April 23 was passed merely to confirm what had been done, or remove any doubt, is in my view stretching things quite a bit.
The minister has drawn an analogy with judicial procedures, but it would seem to me this hardly applies to the case of a minister or agent of the crown when authority has been transferred from one department to another. In this case the minister from whom the powers had been transferred proceeded to sign eight agreements with the provinces, despite the fact that not only did he have no authority to do so, but that authority had been distinctly vested in another minister. The fact that the agreements had to be rescinded and confirmed by the order in council of April 23 seems to me to be something much more than mere confirmation. Indeed, it appears to me that this is tacit acknowledgement on the part of the government that the minister erred in signing these agreements when he had no legal authority to do so-that he was in error when he exercised functions which were vested for those 17 days in the Minister of Forestry.
I do not think there is any value in labouring the matter further. The Minister of Justice has done his best to deal with the situation, but I think we should not deceive ourselves that the order in council of April 23 was merely intended to confirm what had been done and clear up any doubt. I think there can be no doubt at all that the Minister of Agriculture who signed these agreements had no authority to do so. In these circumstances the Minister of Justice was right in insisting that a new order in council be passed and that the agreements be signed again.

Mr. Chairman, may I just ask one question. I am wondering whether there is still some confusion. Yesterday on orders of the day I asked the Minister of Forestry a question relating to the ARDA program. That question was referred to the ten o'clock adjournment period. At ten o'clock yesterday evening the Minister of Agriculture replied to my question on ARDA. Can the Minister of Justice inform the house why the
Supply-Agriculture
Minister of Agriculture, after the explanation he has given, replied to my question last evening?

Mr. Chairman, in reply to this question, the question of the hon. member seemed to us one which was dealing with some of the ARDA projects. Inasmuch as those projects were included in the agriculture estimates and we indicated, as I did also this morning, that this was the way they would be handled, I replied to the question yesterday.
Then are we to discuss the ARDA estimates as included in the estimates of the minister and not refer them to the Minister of Forestry?

The hon. member realizes, of course, that the Minister of Forestry is ill and that these projects do happen to be in my estimates, and have been for some time prior to this. I am quite prepared to answer any questions about them, or if the minister is back he will answer them.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam I do not think there is any point now in labouring this particular issue, but I think we should leave very clear on the record and in the minds of members of the committee that in this warfare which was going on during the month of February between the ministers dividing up the various parts of the corpus delicti, the Department of Agriculture, certain things were done which the Minister of Justice now confesses did create grave doubts in his mind, both with regard to the signing of the eight ARDA agreements by a minister who had no power to sign them, and second with regard to the transfer of one of the senior officials of the Department of Agriculture to the Department of Forestry who carried on certain functions during this interregnum.
I notice that the Leader of the Opposition asked the government when these discussions took place earlier if they would not pass an order in council ratifying all these acts which have taken place in order to make legal what the ministers had done in error, and whether the shifting of one member from one department to another had not created a very doubtful situation. All of these acts should be ratified by order in council. I think that what the minister is telling us is that in the actions which were taken, and in the April 23 order in council which followed those doubtful acts of the minister namely signing certain documents which he had no power to sign, and all of the actions of the official to whom

Supply-Agriculture
we are referring during the interregnum, have now been ratified by that order in council.
In bringing this matter before the house as the Leader of the Opposition requested, the minister is now following the suggestion which has been made, which I think adds up to this. In the haste to make these adjustments between the departments, and in pushing certain sections of the Department of Agriculture one way and then pushing them back the other way, the government has stumbled into a very serious mistake. In their haste they have made these mistakes and now they have to backtrack. I think we should make it clear to the committee and on the record that the government have now put themselves into a mess on a subject they did not know very much about, as a result of which this order in council had to be passed to rectify the situation, and in so doing they accepted the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition.

Mr. Chairman, before the hon. member goes on with his speech one point which arises from what the Minister of Agriculture said in answer to a question a moment ago. While it is true that the ARDA estimates are in the Department of Agriculture-because I presume this transfer had not been made prior to the estimates being drafted- I think the committee ought to insist that those estimates which deal with ARDA be held until the minister responsible for them is here. I think we have a right to hear his statement and to question him regarding the programs he is proposing for the coming year.
I am sure there will be no objection to this.

Mr. Chairman, in order that there will be no misunderstanding may I say that I was happy to grant the courtesy to the Minister of Justice to interrupt my speech on the agriculture estimates so that he could make a very important statement; and in the event that the Leader of the Opposition should ask the same co-operation I would be most happy to grant him a similar courtesy.
In the seven minutes for which I held the floor prior to the luncheon recess I was drawing to the attention of hon. members my view that we were not going to be able to resolve agricultural problems in Canada until we had a general national agricultural policy. In arriving at the same it had to be considered in relationship to the economic system as it now operates in Canada.

In those seven minutes I made reference very briefly to the previous speaker who was not so long ago a minister of agriculture when the Conservatives were in power. I do not believe in discrimination, so I would not like to make reference to a previous agricultural minister without making reference to the present one. It may seem unusual and strange that I, as a private member on the opposition side of the house, should like to ask a favour of the present Minister of Agriculture. My favour is that before the first item of his estimates carries he does what he did not do when he opened his remarks this morning, and inform the members of this committee from his vast store of knowledge on agriculture, under his responsibility as Minister of Agriculture, of his views on a Canadian agricultural policy and what he hopes to do to bring this policy into being.
In the few minutes prior to the luncheon adjournment I was introducing my remarks by pointing out that emergency measures will not solve the problem of our economy in general and of agriculture in particular. I pointed out that we were rapidly moving, and have been for a number of years, from what is normally known as a private enterprise economy towards a subsidized economy. I outlined very briefly a few points of general economy and then I said that I should like to speak about subsidized agriculture. I submit that this government and the preceding government failed to bring about a national agriculture policy and to face up to the real issues.
If hon. members will refer to the estimates in front of them, which are for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1965, they will find there are agricultural subsidies in the estimates. In brief what are they? There are hog quality premiums amounting to $7,599,300; lamb quality premiums, $753,360; cheese quality premiums, $1,083,000; miscellaneous livestock improvement assistance, $16,000; lime assistance, $1,608,900; freight assistance, western feed grains, $18,500,000. These are the direct subsidies in the estimates, but that is only a very small part of the agricultural assistance program. It is not possible to get any figure as to what this assistance will be in the present fiscal year because the majority of agricultural subsidies are not in the estimates; they are covered by statutory authority. It is my understanding-and this information was received only today from the Department of Agriculture-that it is hoped it will not be too high on eggs and hogs because the selling price may be above what is known, I believe, as the support price.

Let us examine the situation and take, for example, butter. I believe my information is correct, that on May 1 the government will announce what its butter policy is going to be in regard to deficiency payments and support price. Last year it was 12 cents per pound. Butter production last year amounted to 345 million pounds; so by statutory payment the butter subsidy cost the federal government in the neighbourhood of $42 million. I do not believe that the majority of members understand that because of a bits and pieces agricultural policy over the years we now have a subsidized agricultural policy in Canada. I base that remark on the Agricultural Stabilization Act, chapter 22, Statutes of Canada 1957-58. How many people realize that private enterprise does not seem to work very much more in agriculture, and this is a basic and absolutely vital and fundamental part of our economy.
May I very, very briefly, for the information of hon. members, deal with this matter. I cannot give what might be estimated for 1964-65, but I refer to the fiscal year 1963-64. How many hon. members know how much the federal government, through its taxation, is tied up in the maintenance of agriculture? During the fiscal year 1963-64 the prices of the following commodities were stabilized under the act:	creamery butter; Cheddar
cheese; cattle; oats-not under the Canadian wheat board; barley-not under the Canadian wheat board. Those commodities were stabilized by purchase. Then by deficiency payment: eggs; hogs; sheep, lamb; sheep, wool; honey; soybeans; sunflower seed; sugar beets; wheat-not under the Canadian wheat board. By subsidy payments: milk for cheese-this is statutory, by the way-milk for butter and butterfat content; cream, butterfat content; dried casein and caseinates, and tobacco. The total amount involved was $122,235,000-and that is statutory.
I ask hon. members to consider these items and the amount involved. This is no longer an emergency policy, but subsidies paid year by year on a continuing basis. How can we be honest in saying we are tackling the problems of agriculture in view of the figures I have given, and what is contained in the estimates with regard to the amount paid by way of subsidy. The problem of agriculture is not going to be solved by a subsidy policy; we have to get down to the basic and fundamental problem. If I had unlimited time, which I have not, I would point out what the statutory and estimates payments actually mean, because in agriculture we have a complete conflict in policy.
Supply-Agriculture
Last year we subsidized butter, at the rate of 12 cents per pound, to the extent of $42 million. That is understandable; I voted for it on the original bill. But at the same time we subsidize soybeans, which are used in the production of margarine. Therefore our subsidy on butter is a persecution of the soybean industry concerned with the production of margarine. We are subsidizing both, and to my mind that is a bunch of damned nonsense.
How would you do it?

I would have a real understanding of agricultural policy in Canada, tying in all agricultural aspects in all phases from the Pacific ocean to the Atlantic. Let us have a national agricultural policy. I think it is nonsense that within Canada we are in conflict agriculturally. We subsidize soybeans and we subsidize the dairy industry in regard to production of a similar product. We have in British Columbia the most marvellous fruit growing area. We grow apples, and they grow apples in Ontario and Nova Scotia. Why do we have this competition? Why do we not have understanding and a Canadian agricultural plan whereby we produce the right things in the places best suited to producing them. In that way we would have unity, efficiency, and the most competitive price possible with which to face the markets of the world.
This basically is my presentation, Mr. Chairman. But you can carry it on. I wonder how many million eggs or how many pounds of powdered eggs we have in Canada now that the taxpayers are paying for by way of support prices. We have so many million pounds of butter that they cannot even hold it in cold storage and have to make butter oil. What can we do with it? We cannot even give it away unless we supply the steamship bottoms in which to send it. In the hungry thirties they burned coffee in the South American states. I should like to know why we are spending millions and millions of dollars for no basic beneficial result. If we tried to give it away, what would be the answer? This government and previous governments have tried to give away some of our surplus produce for which the Canadian taxpayers are paying. What happened immediately this government or previous governments tried to do this? It was said, "You are interfering with our normal market". So you're damned if you do, and you're damned if you don't.
Surely, sir, it is time we got down to some serious thinking, some serious planning. If I may be a bit crude, it is not going to take

Supply-Agriculture
just straight courage; it is going to take a lot of political, governmental and agricultural guts to face up to this problem. It is going to mean governmental control so that uneconomic farms are not established or the operators are moved into economic areas, and so that we do not pay subsidies and deficiency payments only to destroy food. Surely to God we do not have to destroy or waste our butter, powdered milk or canned pork when hundreds of millions of people in the world are starving today. Surely we have got enough sense-[DOT]
Will the hon. member permit a question?

In one moment, please. Surely we have enough sense, or should have as members of parliament, as farmers and as citizens of Canada to try to work out a logical solution to our problems in order to obtain the greatest efficiency so that we can compete in world markets and so that if we have surpluses we will not waste them but use them to feed the hungry people of the world.
I am not necessarily recommending a royal commission. Sometimes I think that royal commissions are a form of escapism for governments. If you have a problem, appoint a royal commission. It will take two, three or four years to complete its work and you will be safe. It will take a year to consider its report and you will be safe. It will take another year to move on one or two or three or four recommendations. Royal commissions are a method of escape. I know the problem cannot be solved in a month or even in a year or two years. But I say to members of the house on this first item of the estimates of the Department of Agriculture that a permanent system of subsidies is no answer to the problems of our economy or to the problems of agriculture.
The other place has been having a holiday while we have not. They do not have enough work to do, but I can think of four times when committees of the other place have done a marvellous job of investigation and study. I suggest that consideration might be given to setting up of a committee of the other place or a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate. Let that committee be given all the technical assistance and money they need and instruct them to make a study of all the various phases of agriculture in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and the position of agriculture in relation to the rest of the economy. Let them then make a report to both houses of parliament and the government in office as to how we can find a permanent solution, a national agricultural policy for Canada that will really

mean something and will place our agriculturalists, whether they are engaged in mixed farming or are dairy farmers, soybean growers or growers of any other crop, in their proper relationship to the economy of Canada generally. In this way we will be able to guarantee our farmers security and comparability of income with professional people in Canada on a basis of completely efficient operation from production to marketing. In this way Canada would be able to compete in world markets as one of the greatest and finest agricultural countries in the universe.

Will the hon. member permit a question? I wonder whether he is speaking for the New Democratic party or merely for himself when he advises, as he has, that agricultural subsidies should be done away with.

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but apparently the hon. member has either not been here or has not listened to what I said in the seven minutes I spoke before one o'clock, and what I have said since. Not once but three times I have stated that in my 11 years as a member of this house I have on every occasion supported subsidies for every aspect of agriculture. I have also said that I support them now. But my point is that subsidies are not the answer to the problems of agriculture in our country. I say that we should get down to real study and planning for a national agricultural policy, so that in the long run we can get away from subsidies for agriculture. Let us plan so that agriculture can take its rightful place in the Canadian economy.

Would the hon. member tell the committee how his party would suggest that the farmers be coerced into growing what his all-brainy and all-knowing planners would decide they should grow in a particular region of Canada?
Oh, come, come; you are having a pipe dream.

I have been asked a question so I shall answer it. May I tell my hon. friend he may have a different idea of himself but my name is Winch, not Moses. I do not know all the problems; I do not know all the answers. I very rarely speak in this way, but may I say that I had the honour of being elected a member of the legislature of British Columbia for 20 years. I have been here for 11 years and, by God, there are not very many who have had 31 years in parliament undefeated. I put forward the problem as I see it and I make recommendations as to how I think we might tackle the problem.

Nobody in Canada can be coerced as long as we have a parliamentary democracy, because if the electors are not satisfied they can throw you out at the next election. They have not thrown me out yet.
Does the hon. member suggest he is the right man to lead his party into the promised land?
I am a follower, not a leader.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a word or two about the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver East. First, however, 1 should like to join with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle in expressing my congratulations to the Minister of Agriculture for the change that has taken place in the thinking of the department with respect to research, the end results of money which is spent on exhibitions and so on.
I think that some of the things that the hon. member for Vancouver East has suggested are very worth while. I agree with him when he says that we should have a policy that will allow agriculture in Canada to reach what might be termed the optimum of production, that will allow us to distribute food to the hungry people of the world where-ever it is needed, and that we should do away with the conflict or what appears to be conflict in subsidies for the production of certain products. When he calls for a study of the problem I agree with him, but may I also say that it is probably the most perplexing problem in the world and one which is not confined to Canada.
We know, for example, that just a few months ago agricultural policy as it relates to trade between nations, particularly in Europe, almost caused the European economic community to dissolve. So the problem of distributing agricultural products and foodstuffs is a very large one and it has created far greater ramifications in other parts of the world than it has in Canada.
I should like also to remind him, and I do not do this to take anything away from the objectives he outlined, that the government of the United States has spent several billions of dollars over the last two years to support the price of farm products. After large quantities of food products were in a surplus supply position, the United States tried many ways of distributing it throughout the world. They tried selling it at reduced prices. They tried long term credits. They even came to the position where they sold large quantities of it and took what was called soft currencies in return, but left those currencies in the countries in which the food was sold
Supply-Agriculture
for development purposes. I am not sure of the reason for this, but it does not seem to me the United States has made a large number of friends by following this kind of policy. There may be other implications. I mention these things only to point out this is a very complex problems. While we may agree with the objectives, I am sure there is going to be a lot of disagreement on how to reach those objectives.
We have not had any suggestions from the minister on how to reach them.

I agree. I was going to say that I congratulate the minister upon some of the things he said with regard to some changes he proposed in connection with research exhibitions and so on. However, I was a little disappointed in the lack of some evidence of new policy with regard to what he was going to do about the depressed condition of agriculture in eastern Canada, and what he was going to do about moving some of the surpluses we have of butter, eggs and a few other things.
There is one very important change, Mr. Chairman, in what the Minister of Agriculture had to say today, and that is the attitude of the Liberal party toward the percentage of the national income farmers receive. I was very pleased indeed to hear the minister say that the Department of Agriculture now only takes about 3 per cent of the total national budget, and this was a very small amount indeed when compared to the contribution agriculture makes to the economy and to the well being of Canadians. I was pleased also to hear him say that there is a false impression in the minds of many Canadians that farmers are getting more than their fair share of the national income and of the federal government's budget. I suggest that if he has made this change in his own thinking, he should inform some of his colleagues, particularly those from the urban areas of Ontario, that this is now government policy.
During the last two election campaigns at least, these people did go about the province of Ontario telling the electors that when a new Liberal government came to power they would see the farmers did not get too much from the federal government. I think the minister should tell the Prime Minister that this is the policy. I recall very vividly not long ago that in a speech in Ontario the Prime Minister said one of the things his government would do would be to see that the $200 acreage bonus was no longer paid. I am not going to argue the merits or demerits of that bonus, but I do say that the statement probably was made for the political impact it

Supply-Agriculture
would have, and that impact was to alienate some of the urban electors from the government of the day. I am sure it had that effect because the results of the election in 1962 clearly indicated there was a disenchantment with the previous government and perhaps a large portion of it was the result of the charge that the Conservative government was paying far too much attention to the rural areas.
I agree with what the Minister of Agriculture said today, because 3 per cent of the national budget is a very small amount for the farmers to receive when one thinks of the contribution the farmers make in producing foodstuffs for the country. As the minister has said, we do have a very high standard of living. I should like to point out also that it is true there were some cash payments out of the national budget during those years from 1957 or 1958 to 1962. I do not want to go over a lot of history, but I say that from 1946 until 1953 or 1954, the farmers producing grain in the western provinces certainly had a lot of consideration coming to them from the people of Canada for having accepted substantially less for their products than those products were selling on the world market. This is an old story that has been told many times, but it is still valid today.
To get back to this matter of research, I may say I am pleased the minister is now going to put more emphasis on the utility and practical value that can come from the research stations across Canada. I know he has appointed an advisory committee to sit in at meetings with the officials of the Manyberries range station. I agree that this is a good idea. I should like to offer some suggestions to him and to this committee because the Manyberries range station happens to be in my constituency. I know this station has, in fact, developed many new methods for range management using some new varieties of seed, and that is very beneficial to all areas of the prairie provinces. One of the problems is that there has been a tendency on the part of farmers and ranchers not to make use of this information and actually apply it to their own operation.
I have a number of reports here from the Manyberries range station. This station has proven conclusively that the use of tame grasses such as crested wheatgrass, wild Russian ryegrass and Rambler alfalfa, in conjunction with native grasses actually increases productivity of the land. For example, I have in front of me a publication that was printed at the Manyberries range station in the summer of 1962, which contains a table indicating the total digestive nutrients in three different

types of fodder. In so far as native grass is concerned the table shows the amount consumed contained 69 pounds of total digestible nutrients per acre; the crested wheatgrass contained 144 pounds of total disgestible nutrients, and the Russian wild rye contained 150 pounds of total digestible nutrients per acre. These grasses were grown in exactly the same area, with the same amount of rainfall and with the same fertility so far as the soil is concerned.
In addition to that, Dr. R. W. Lodge, who conducted a number of experiments, states that as a result of seven years of grazing trials they have shown that complementary grazing-a combination of native and tame pastures-will increase annual beef production by at least 50 per cent. They found that li acres of crested wheatgrass, plus eight acres of native grass, carried a yearling for five months of grazing. Where native grass was used alone, it took 16 acres to carry a yearling steer. The complementary grazing produced 35 pounds of beef per acre, as compared to only 20 pounds per acre where only native grass was used.
I wish to point out that the research station at Manyberries has already found out how to double the carrying capacity and how to increase, from 20 pounds to 35 pounds, the production of beef per acre. But unfortunately, in the areas where farmers could make use of this advice, they are not doing that. I suggest that some kind of program be undertaken to make the farmers aware of the results of this test. There is no greater incentive for a farmer to change his method than to let him realize it is profitable to do so.
We have to face some pretty disturbing developments respecting the production of beef in other parts of the world. For example, the United States had had to try to enter into import agreements with Australia, New Zealand and Ireland because these countries have a far lower cost of production per pound of beef and their competition with the United States producer is becoming very severe.
Just a few months ago quite a number of cattlemen in western Canada attended a meeting in Memphis, Tennessee, sponsored by the beef growing organizations in the United States. Many of the, shall I say, cow and calf operators who raised beef on the open range, thought they were pretty efficient producers and could compete with anybody anywhere in the world. But the United States organizations had sent a team to Australia to see what they were doing there, and even the most efficient of the producers on the North American continent became concerned

with the reports that came back. For example, on an actuarial cost calculation it is possible for Australian producers to raise a steer from the time it is born until it is two years old, for $6.80. No one in Canada or the United States can come anywhere near that cost factor.
The Australian steer may not be of the same quality and as big as the Canadian steer, but with modern transportation it is possible for the Australians to send their beef to the North American continent and sell it here for less than half the cost of home production of North American beef.
We know a great deal about how to increase the efficiency of our beef production, but there has been a missing link in getting the farmers to adopt the new procedures and new methods which have been tested and proven satisfactory. I do not want to labour this point any more, except to say that along with the new facilities for research something should be done to encourage ranchers and farmers to make use of the knowledge that has been discovered.
The minister mentioned exhibitions and the change which would be made in government grants for agricultural exhibitions. I agree with him that there should be more emphasis on utility than has been the case in the past. In so far as the prize winners in beef classes are concerned, I suppose the prettiest animal gets the prize, but that does not necessarily mean it is the most efficient, in terms of the feed conversion factor. However, I would suggest that the minister move rather slowly in making changes because we have a long tradition respecting the kind of classes that are judged in these shows, and the people who breed and prepare animals for them will not be able suddenly to change over to a whole new classification.
For this reason I am glad the minister is starting out with a pilot project for Hereford beef cattle, and perhaps by next year something can be done with respect to hogs and sheep.
I did not quite follow the remarks of the minister when he talked about trying to tie research and exhibition policies together. I hope that some time during this debate he will be able to give more explanation of that. Of course I understand that the prizes which will be offered in exhibitions will have the purpose of enhancing and upgrading the practical value of animals developed in Canada, but I did not quite follow his remarks as to how this was to be related to research. I was very interested in his comments that there would be only two classes of bulls, four classes of females, and a completely new
Supply-Agriculture
concept in the classification of the factors that will determine the winners in the steer classes. I shall not go into the detail of these now, but there is a great deal of merit in what the minister said.
With respect to grain, whether it be wheat, oats, barley or any other type, I am pleased the minister will insist that a large quantity of grain be produced to back up the sample that is actually shown to the judges. In many cases the prizes have been given to those persons who have carefully gone through a large amount of grain and picked a select sample from it. If exhibitors were required to show a reasonable, commercial amount of grain to back up their samples, it would be impossible for them to get away with their previous practices, where probably only 5 per cent or 10 per cent of the grower's grain actually looked the same as the samples presented to the judges. Surely, it is only reasonable to expect that what the judges inspect should be representative.
I am glad the minister is supporting and intends to participate in the conference to be held in Montreal later this month to reclassify hogs and try to improve their food conversion rate along with their "cutability"-I think that was the word he used.
There is another point I wish to raise. It was brought up by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and is a very valid point when we are considering agriculture. It is that, perhaps even more important than production, is the question of distribution and marketing. I have long contended that in western Canada, where I know the agricultural establishment best, if at any time there is a guaranteed substantial market for any particular product, whether it be beef, or wheat or barley or anything else, at a price level which will enable the producers to make some money, the farmers, who are very resourceful, will be able to supply the product. We know that in the past three years there has been a substantial and expanding market for wheat. It is true there have been better than average crops and that the good harvests may to a large extent have been due to favourable weather; but at the same time I can assure the minister that if there is a continuing market on the long term basis over say, five years or ten years, the farmers of western Canada could increase the output of wheat still further. Last year it was 720 million bushels. They could easily produce a billion bushels or even more as long as they could sell it at a profit. I believe this is also true of beef.

Supply-Agriculture
Not very long ago the present minister and, indeed, the former minister of agriculture were advocating that people should devote part of their operation to the production of beef. I was concerned at the time that if this movement went too far there would be surpluses and the price of beef would fall, resulting in an unfortunate position for the one commodity which has been helping to maintain the stability of our agricultural economy. That has not happened yet, but there has certainly been a lowering of the price of beef and it is to some extent due to the fact that more and more people are getting into beef production after being encouraged to do so by the minister and by his predecessor in office. So, as I have said, this question of distribution is one of great importance.
Something should be said about the problem of farmers in eastern Canada. As far as we in this party are concerned, we are prepared to support some kind of program which would improve the position of these farmers. We should like to hear some statement on dairy policies. We think this new approach to hog classification and selection is a good move. We have stated on several occasions that we support a policy of getting feed grain into eastern Canada at least at a stabilized price-whether it is higher or lower is something else. But at least these farmers and feeders in eastern Canada should know from one month to the next how much they will have to pay for their feed.
It is easy to say that there are too many farms in eastern Canada which are too small to be efficient, but I know there is an attachment to the land and to the family home which has been built up there over the generations. This is also true of western Canada, but not to the same extent. While understanding this we must face the fact that our farms are becoming larger and that larger farms are more efficient. Perhaps some kind of program could be undertaken to encourage an increase in the acreage of farms in eastern Canada in order to improve the efficiency of their operation. I was pleased to note a few days ago a release from the department informing us that 44 new soil and water conservation projects had been approved for Quebec under the ARDA program. That release was dated April 15. We support this, but we believe the minister should be moving a little faster in some of the other areas. I know that the minister of agriculture for the province of Alberta said only a few days ago that the federal government had acted a little less than fast in approving some of the cost-sharing programs

under ARDA. I do not know why the government has, apparently, not moved as rapidly as the provinces are ready to move. It may be that the federal government has not worked out all the details as to what they intend to include in the projects they would be prepared to approve. In any event, I think the government is moving far too slowly in this matter, though some progress is being made.
In my own constituency there is one project which, I believe, has already been submitted to the federal Department of Agriculture. I suppose, now, it is in the hands of the Department of Forestry. It concerns the establishment of ground water reserves in the southern part of the prairie. We have just gone through a winter during which very little snow has fallen. Consequently there has been very little run-off and the surplus water available for stock watering purposes particularly is at a very low level. I know that the local ARDA committee did recommend that a fairly large program be undertaken to delineate the ground water resources in order that wells could be drilled and stock water brought to the surface.

Mr. Chairman, allow me first of all to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) for the rather interesting statement he made a while ago.
It is gratifying for us to see him so often in the house because it is always pleasant to see that a minister is interested in our work and discussions. I must say that we did deplore the frequent absences of the minister from the house.
But I am still wondering which personage I should admire in our Minister of Agriculture: the minister or the businessman? This afternoon, I am convinced that the Minister of Agriculture is an outstanding businessman. He is also very good at stock farming, especially at beef cattle breeding.

Therefore, his speech was very good as far as his knowledge is concerned, but not quite so good as far as his responsibilities as minister are concerned.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, we were expecting this afternoon to be presented with a general statement on the Liberal party farm policy for the whole of Canada. We, from the province of Quebec, expected something to raise our hopes for some improvement in the status of our agriculture which is now at its lowest level. In fact, if we consider statistics for the last 20 years, we find that, as far as farming is concerned, the western provinces have continually bettered their position while the province of Quebec saw its situation deteriorating more and more, to the point that nowadays, it is on the verge of bankruptcy.
I made those few observations to draw the minister's attention on the real problems facing the province of Quebec. Far be it from me to criticize without rhyme or reason. I simply wish to draw the minister's attention to that situation and tell him that people in my riding and farmers all across the province of Quebec are expecting some action from the federal government. I think that if this government does not take positive steps in 1964, the loss suffered by agriculture in the province of Quebec could not be repaired.
As I said, we were very disappointed this afternoon to hear about cattle trade, beef breeding, international exhibitions and fairs, and finally wheat, and that last point did not surprise us too much. Since I have been in this house, every time agriculture is discussed, in 95 per cent of cases, the discussion has to do with wheat: will farmers be able to sow it, is there going to be enough rain, will they be able to harvest wheat, and finally will it be possible to sell it? All the efforts of the minister are for the wheat business and the products of the other provinces are not discussed in this house.
I would ask the minister-if he has found markets for our cattle as the Minister of Trade and Commerce found some for our wheat, well and good-to devote some of his efforts to try and find markets for the dairy products of the province of Quebec. And let them stop telling us, when we have production surpluses in some fields: cease production, you have too much produce.
If we were going to say that for wheat, Mr. Chairman, what would happen to Canada?
No, we never have too much wheat; we must always have more. The ministers concerned have the responsibility of finding 20220-163
Supply-Agriculture
markets for that product. In the province of Quebec we have too much milk and we are told: stop production. We have too much cheese and we are told: throw it away. We have too many eggs, and we are told: let them go bad. Such are the answers we are given. It is necessary-
Who says that?
Who said that?

I am not talking about the present government, but of what I have been hearing for 50 years.
What strikes me-and you are well aware of the fact-is that we have not had a single minister of agriculture from eastern Canada in the last 50 years. In all fairness we should at least be given one from the east from time to time. You people from the west have had them all for the last 50 years, while we did not even have one. We are asking for a minister from the east, and we are a bit disappointed at not getting one.
The minister does not seem to realize what serious problems eastern farmers are up against, and especially those in Quebec. He acts as if only western Canada existed and he is quite shocked when he is asked, and I am quoting him: "What do you do with the money we send you in the west?"
That is what the minister said this afternoon. In my opinion, that question, which he put to the house, is the most interesting part of his speech.
I admit that if western Canada is very prosperous today it is due to the joint programs. But it must be remembered that all those joint programs are paid for by taxes on a pro rata basis according to the population of each province. Forty years ago the country's two largest provinces, that is Quebec and Ontario, agreed to take part in these programs to help economically weak provinces. They were happy to do it, sure that their sacrifices would benefit them later.
Today, things are different; the poorer provinces have become prosperous, at least they have means of subsistence. Therefore, it is no longer urgent to assist them. That is why we maintain that a number of joint programs should be done away with. Besides, that was a promise made by the Liberal party.
I should like to call every hon. member's attention on this matter of joint programs in order to readjust this assistance according to present needs. To prove my point, I would ask the minister to look at the latest

Supply-Agriculture
publication about federal-provincial conditional grants under joint programs. I received this publication recently and I was greatly interested in it. I urge all those interested in agriculture, as well as all those interested in joint programs in general, to read it. You will see that, very often, the claims of the province of Quebec are well founded if you study calmly the distribution of those joint programs. Just to mention a few lines, I will simply take the Department of Agriculture, at page 11, the part dealing with manpower: joint program on manpower.
In 1961-62, total benefits for the province of Quebec were $21,000.
This is what agricultural joint programs yielded under the agreements; Prince Edward Island, $21,000; Nova Scotia, $130,000; New Brunswick, $61,659; Quebec, $287,560; Ontario, $1,213,982; Manitoba, $290,697; Alberta, $837,442; and British Columbia, $390,899.
If you take into account the population figures for each province or if you figure those grants on a pro rata basis, you will see that they are not advantageous for Quebec.
Another joint program concerns the federal government contribution toward the transportation cost of cattle to the Royal Winter Fair, and the Minister of Agriculture is familiar with that. In that field, the federal government reimburses 75 per cent of the cost borne by the provinces; there again, western Canada gets the highest grants.
Grants are somewhat to the advantage of Quebec in one field and that is in the assistance provided in the case of agricultural lime.
I am quoting those figures in order to kill two birds with one stone; I want to prove that compared to the other provinces, Quebec needs more assistance in this regard. Federal grants are distributed as follows: Newfoundland, $18,313; Prince Edward Island, $71,457; Nova Scotia, $115,526; New Brunswick, $106,487; Quebec, $2,236,648; Ontario, $436,536; British Columbia, $74,500.
This clearly shows the poor quality of Quebec farms. As a matter of fact, there are no payments for the western provinces which have been built up, so to speak, thanks to these joint programs. If I quote these figures, it is simply to prove that there should not be any joint programs for provinces that do not need them in the least, now.
During 1961-62, the federal government paid a subsidy of $217,040 to the province of Manitoba for damming and drainage works in the Riding and Duck Mountain basin.

As far as Saskatchewan is concerned, the federal government spent there until March 31, 1961, the sum of $2,208,853 for the development of the Pasquia area along the Saskatchewan river.
Mr. Chairman, it should be noted that those are all joint programs for the sole benefit of the western provinces; Quebec gets nothing.
In the same province again, and until March 31, 1962, the federal government spent $30,165,796 for irrigation and power works with respect to the South Saskatchewan river.
Now to revert to the maritime provinces, it was found that the federal government spent a total amount of $311,305 under the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act.
Still in the field of joint programs, we come now to ARDA. In my opinion, it is the plan which might have been of the greatest benefit to the province of Quebec. As a matter of fact, it has finally been realized that the few possibilities we had were not used. Last year, an amount of $111,000 was spent, and, this year, about $1,500,000 will be spent for land drainage alone.
In answer to the question I asked last year, I was told that the western provinces had received $179,000. At last we are going to receive this year an amount of $1 million under joint programs.
Mr. Chairman, I do not want to criticize the western provinces, but I merely want to set the record straight, so that the value of ARDA might be judged.
Recently, the Department of Forestry issued a release in which one could read:
"Four different programs under the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act (ARDA) provide for the extension and development of pastures along the forest line in northern Saskatchewan", says a joint announcement by federal Minister of Forestry Maurice Sauve, and Saskatchewan Minister of Agriculture I. C. Nollet. A fifth project which has been approved for the province of Saskatchewan provides for the continuation of a drainage and flood control program.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are the advantages which have been granted to the western provinces.
Quebec might have more particularly last year, benefited from ARDA to a greater extent if the farmers had been offered greater advantages with regard to agriculture.
But what did actually happen? To get the right picture we only need to look up the list or the number of farm credit counsellors who advise the farmers in each area. Those advisors on farm credit might have made us benefit to a greater extent from ARDA, in connection with our land.
And how are the farm counsellors distributed? In British Columbia there are six, in

Alberta 32, in Saskatchewan 36, in Manitoba 12, in Ontario 35, and only four in Quebec. The same situation prevails in almost every field. But, even considering only the agricultural sector, I think that I have quoted enough figures to indicate to this government that if it does not wake up and straighten out things soon, it is useless for the taxpayers of Quebec to pay taxes, just to starve on their land.
The federal government paid $58,856 to the western provinces in premiums for pedigreed breeding stock.
The federal government even subsidizes sow breeding contests. It is true that the subsidy is not very high but New Brunswick and Manitoba did receive $1,705.
In 1961-62, the federal government spent $203,269, that is $140,745 in Manitoba, $37,864 in Saskatchewan and $24,600 in British Columbia, to encourage the construction of storage facilities for potatoes. On the other hand, Quebec did not get a cent. However, at last a little money is going to be spent there in 1964.
As far as crop insurance is concerned, I do not remember exactly the statistics, since I asked for such data last year. As Quebec is not participating in this scheme it did not receive anything, but the Quebec taxpayers pay federal taxes just the same.
For the fiscal year 1961-62, the federal government spent the sum of $193,932 for crop insurance in Manitoba.
As for the drilling of community wells under the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, the federal government pays 35 per cent of the cost.
Considering the grants paid as indemnity for losses caused by disease, it is found that during 1961-62, the federal government paid $12,814, but that Quebec did not receive a cent.
Now let us speak about the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act.
Up to March 31, 1962, the federal government paid $23,550,036 for the St. Mary river irrigation project. As for the Bow river project, the federal government spent $30,577,445, of which $2,400,000 was to purchase the assets of the company that had undertook this project.
The eastern irrigation district, that is the former Brooks district, in Alberta, received a federal contribution of $35,793 in 1959-60 and of $83,449 in 1960-61.
Let us take a closer look at the situation with regard to the feed grain transportation assistance. In 1958-59, Saskatchewan and Alberta received $183,623 and $46,976 in 1959-60, for a grand total of $230,599, while 20220-163J
Supply-Agriculture
the province of Quebec got nothing at all.
Now, let us consider another project. In 1959-60 and 1960-61, in view of the poor harvesting conditions which prevailed in the prairie provinces, the federal government spent $316,972.
On June 27, 1961, in view of the extreme drought of that year, the federal government offered the prairie provinces to pay half the amounts they had spent and then disbursed the sum of $1,091,604.
Let us consider now the matter of transportation of seed grain in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. The government agreed to pay back 75 per cent of the freight charges.
Under the heading of emergency assistance with regard to unharvested crops, we learn that the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba received a total amount of $6,182,452. And so forth, Mr. Chairman.
We could give enough proof to put an end to the contention that we, Quebeckers, are always criticizing or speaking without rhyme or reason. We do not speak without rhyme or reason; we make claims in order to balance the position of the province of Quebec with regard to that of other provinces. In my opinion, this can only be done by establishing a department of agriculture for the east, and this is what I want to deal with.
The project of establishing a department of agriculture for the east has been given up, but I believe that we should reconsider it. I then ask the Minister of Agriculture to examine this question because it is the only way we can solve the agricultural problem in the east.
We need a department that will try to improve agricultural conditions so that our farmers may know a certain degree of prosperity after giving so much in taxes over the last 35 years to the western provinces. Now that their agriculture is well organized, we should get the opportunity to reorganize ours.
Right now we are a little like the father who has given too much to his children. We gave too much and we are still giving a lot to the western provinces in taxes of all kinds. That is why we ask you, with regard to joint programs, to give us back our taxing powers, so that we may give a new lease on life to our agriculture, after contributing to the development of agriculture throughout Canada and giving it that impetus about which we boast everywhere.
Let us give Quebec farmers a chance to rebuild their economy and regain the control of their own business. That is why it is urgent to give them competent men and especially financial means. Let us put an end to the programs which benefit Quebec only

Supply-Agriculture
in a proportion of 32 per cent whereas our province's share of taxes is paid on the basis of its population.
That is why I advocate the repeal of such taxes. If the Minister of Agriculture, being the businessman he is, took the trouble of treating eastern farmers not as farmers but as businessmen, if he prefers, I am sure he would be aware of the pitiful condition of agriculture in our part of the country. If he is sincere and responsible, he will strive to make Canada a place where it is good to live because for the past 30 years we from Quebec have done our share to make this country the bread basket of the world as far as wheat is concerned.
Let us have the opportunity to recover the little that is left to us, to rebuild our strength and to take our place among the other provinces so that Quebec may once again be for Canada the asset it was 30 or 35 years ago.

Before I was unnecessarily interrupted I was about to say that I would have expected the Minister of Agriculture, in opening the debate on his estimates, to tell the committee, and through the committee the farmers of Canada, what he intends to do to meet some of their most pressing problems, particularly what he intends to do to implement some of the pledges which the government made to the farmers of Canada last year in the election campaign. The minister made a very excellent speech, if it were being delivered to a fair board, on how to raise better livestock, how to improve certain varieties of grain and how to get better production on certain kinds of soil, all of which is very useful, and I compliment him on his knowledge in these fields. But the minister has not told the committee or the farmers what he proposes to do about their most pressing problem, the problem of farm income.
Supply-A griculture
If the farmers could get a price that is commensurate with their costs of production, the minister would not have any trouble about getting farmers to co-operate in producing a better class of livestock, in experimenting with new varieties of grain, new types of fertilizer and increasing their production. The farmers of the prairie provinces have proven that. As soon as the wheat board was able to sell wheat, the farmers soon demonstrated they could grow wheat. As soon as this government demonstrates they can help the farmer rectify his income problem, there will be no problem about getting farmers to increase their production. 1 say the central problem facing farmers in all parts of Canada today is the problem of farm income.
The dominion bureau of statistics figures show that real income per farm in 1951 was $2,641; in 1952, it was $2,656. From then on, it was below that and considerably below that. In 1954, it went down to $1,890 and only exceeded the 1952 figures in 1961 when it rose to $2,755. In 1962 it was $3,144, which is an all time high. This was the cash income per farm. The dominion bureau of statistics shows that when these figures are adjusted into constant 1951 dollars, the farm income in 1951 was $2,641 and stayed below that, every year until 1962 when it was $2,487. In other words, we have never since 1951 reached, in constant dollars, the per farm income of 1951, namely, $2,641. In terms of what a dollar will buy, farm income is lower now than it was in 1951. The last figures which were published for 1963 show that total farm cash income is up by 2.2 per cent, but that the net income for the farmer is only up in two provinces and is down in every other province.
The real measurement of the farmer's prosperity cannot be measured by looking at his income, either his net income or his cash income. At the same time you have to look at what it costs him to produce. If one takes a look at the index commodity figure for the things which the farmers has to buy in order to produce, one finds that in 1951 it was 230 and in 1962 it had climbed to 290. This is a fabulous increase in price of the things the farmer buys. The dominion bureau of statistics shows that the index commodity figure for the things a farmer had to sell in 1951 was 296 and in 1962 it had dropped to 264.
The real problem, therefore, facing agriculture is that while the prices which the farmer receives for the products he produces have gone down, the prices of the things which he must buy in order to produce have gone up at an amazing rate. This is why agriculture faces a serious problem. I say that

Supply-Agriculture
before we pass this item the committee should insist that we have some statement from the minister referring to the matters which he outlined to us last year. He said the government was going to take some action to reduce the price of farm machinery. I remember asking him some questions last year: What was the government going to do to reduce these prices; was there going to be an investigation by an agriculture committee of the house; what steps had the government in mind to bring prices down because agricultural implements constitute for farmers, the most important item in their cost of production?
This is not only true of farm implements, it is equally true of other things which the farmer must buy, such as his pesticides and fertilizers. A great many of the commodities which the farmer buys have gone up in price, while the price he receives for his products in constant dollars has gone down. The minister, it seems to me, ought to tell the committee what he is going to do about farm costs.
The minister told us also last session that he was going to introduce some legislation to help farmers get credit. As everyone recognizes, agriculture now is highly capitalized and it requires larger amounts of capital for equipment, for land, for buildings, for mechanization and for many of the materials that are necessary for production. This means the average farmer is suffering from the problem of under-capitalization. When the minister talked today about improving stock and improving farming methods, what ought to be kept in mind is that all of this costs money. A farmer cannot improve his production, he cannot improve his farm methods unless he is able to get the necessary capital to carry out such a program.
I think we should have a statement from the minister as to what the government's plans are with reference to farm credit. I believe we should have a statement also with reference to crop insurance. Last year during the election campaign the Liberal party referred often to reinsurance in connection with crop insurance plans. It is undoubtedly true that too large a share of the responsibility has been left with the few provincial governments who have co-operated with the federal government in setting up crop insurance plans. Reinsurance would be a partial solution. Is the minister going to bring in legislation for reinsurance under the crop insurance plan? If he is, I think we should be told about it, or he should put it on the order paper so we could know before these

estimates are passed whether the government was merely talking last year during the election or whether it intends to carry out the promises it made.
Most important of all, I think we need to know something about the government's intention with regard to setting up national marketing boards, about which it talked a great deal during the last federal election. One of the very specific promises that was made was uttered by the Prime Minister on March 7, 1963 in the city of Saskatoon when he told the farmers of western Canada that in lieu of acreage payments, which the Liberal party were going to discontinue, it was the intention of the Liberal party if elected to compensate the farmer in two ways: First of all, to institute the two price system for wheat and, second, by guaranteeing to the farmers by means of deficiency payments, $2 per bushel for No. 1 wheat, basis Fort William. We have not had a single word as to whether the government intends to proceed with this very specific commitment made by the Prime Minister, and echoed and re-echoed by the Liberal candidates all over western Canada.
The indications are that the price of wheat is declining. For the last crop year the average price for all grain worked out at about $1.65 a bushel as compared with $1.68 a bushel for the previous crop year.
