subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF AGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, George Bernard Shaw is reputed to have said that youth is a wonderful thing, but it is too bad it is wasted on young people. The qualities of youth which were so attractive to George Bernard Shaw are qualities which do not apply only to young people. Our conception of age, longevity of life-all these things are changes, and we have to adjust our view to the changing worries and facts of our society. One of the stark realities of life in twentieth century Canada is that for people 65 years and over two chief factors, are poverty and loneliness.
We are dealing today, Mr. Speaker, with a bill to assist the absorption of older people into the labour market. I think we should look at the composition of the population of Canada today. Half of the Canadian population is under 25 years of age; 7.8 per cent or 7.9 20220-164
24. 1964	2571
Canada Fair Employment Practices Act per cent are over 65 years of age. One half of the population supports the other half. An analysis of the trends in population reveals that by 1971 the percentage of persons in the 30 to 40 age group will have shrunk.
The essential needs of old people are not any different from those of any other age group, except in degree. As of March 31, 1963, the percentage of recipients of old age assistance to the population in the 65 to 69 years of age group ranged from 13.12 per cent in a relatively prosperous province like Ontario to 52.93 per cent in Newfoundland. That is from roughly one in eight to better than one in two of that age group. A very considerable number of the aged live in inadequate housing, are ill-fed, insufficiently cared for medically, and deprived of opportunities for normal social intercourse and recreation. The problem of absorbing older people in the employment stream is a reflection of the general level of employment in Canada. When there are enough jobs to go around, then the problem of the aged is less acute. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the entire problem of older people must be viewed in terms of the rate of economic growth of our country.
There are a number of illusions about older workers. I believe that this bill is a palliative but that the illusions are much more serious and are matters with which we must deal if we really want to tackle this problem. About 33 per cent of the unemployed persons in Canada at any given time are over 40 years of age. Many experience long periods of unemployment. Many older persons are refused interviews for jobs because company policy restricts hiring of personnel over the age of 35 or even as low as 30. In a study made of 950 classified advertisements in a group of newspapers, it was found that 490 or more than 51 per cent stated age restrictions. Only 18 of those advertising were willing to accept applicants up to 50 years of age.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what are some of these illusions about older workers? One of them is that among older people you have a higher frequency of illness and therefore greater absenteeism. Another illusion is that physical deterioration is synonymous with age and therefore older people are more accident prone. Another illusion is that age has a direct bearing on insurance rates, and therefore the costs of pension plans mount successively with each new participant over 40 years of age. It is said-and this is a very serious matter-that as people grow older their ability to learn decreases, and it is therefore more difficult to train older people in new industrial methods and techniques. There is a myth that a
2572	HOUSE OF
Canada Fair Employment Practices Act man over 40 is not as productive as he was at 20. The myth of the older worker has no firm basis in truth. Chronological age is not a sound foundation on which to build hiring policies. It gives no indication of a man's ability or his skills and knowledge, the important elements to be considered when people are hired.
A study was undertaken by the economics and research branch of the Department of Labour covering 1,018 employees in two large department stores in two Canadian cities, and this study was the first of its kind in the field. It was found, Mr. Speaker, that those qualities which make for good salesmanship are not exclusively the property of any age group. Flexibility, adaptability and other traits which make a person a preferred employee and which bring a profit to a firm exist in all age groups. Further, the report showed that sales performance improves somewhere between the ages of 51 and 55 and declines slowly in the ensuing years. The record of performance of people past 40 is as good as that of other employees, if not better. The sales clerk employed after age 40 attained a higher performance rating within a shorter period of service than a younger employee. Workers hired after the age of 40 tend to outperform those hired below the age of 30. The older workers attained a higher performance rating within a shorter period of time. This represents savings for companies which would otherwise have spent money on training. In all cases the average score for employees over the age of 60 compared favourably with that of employees below the age of 51.
Performance was below average in the case of employees under 31 years of age, and about average in the case of employees between 31 and 40. The best average in the case of employees was over 46 years of age. The best performance in store A related to employees in the age group 51 to 55; in store B, to those in the late 50's.
Mr. Speaker, there is also the question of labour turnover, which involves an enormous cost for industry. It has been found that there is less turnover in more mature workers than in younger workers. The worker of 45 and over quits his job less than one half as often as the younger worker. Similarly but to a less marked degree, the older worker is fired from his job less often than the younger worker. A 12-month survey in seven cities in the United States covering establishments employing 3.9 million workers showed that if an older worker obtains a regular job lasting at least one year, he is more likely than a younger person to stay [Mr. Gelber.l

with the firm up to the age of normal retirement. The annual separation rate for all groups was 54 for each 100 workers employed at the end of the pediod under study. The rate was 62 per 100 for those persons under 45 years of age. In contrast, the rate for those over 45 was 38 separations per 100 employees. This indicates that older employees are better employment risks than younger employees.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is the myth about learning ability. A scientific study was undertaken in the United States concerning the intellectual ability to absorb. The army alpha intelligence test was administered to 127 male freshmen at Iowa State College during 19181919. It was readministered to the same group after an interval of 31 years, during 1949-50. In analysing the results, psychologists took into consideration the effects of social background, experience and the other factors which might have a bearing on the better scores attained in the 1950 tests. The net result was that it was found that the group was intellectually more able at 50 than they were in 1919.
Dr. Margaret Mead, the famous sociologist has said that "to put all the learning into childhood, all the work into middle age and all the regrets into old age" is one of the illusions of our society. It is time that society accepted the fact that it is possible to learn at any age and that learning ability is not the exclusive property of any age group. A program of education, based on the findings that older workers are flexible, can adapt themselves to new techniques and new ideas, should be highly successful in bringing about the reduction of age prejudice and the end of hiring restrictions.
Another factor, Mr. Speaker, is the question of pensions. We all know that the Canada pension plan, which this parliament will surely enact and which will give to all workers a portable pension, will destroy this one further obstacle to the employment of older workers. It seems to me that what we have to do in dealing with this problem is to educate industry, to educate employers, to educate the public into the idea that the illusions we have about older workers being costly, are harmful and are inequitable in terms of the growing group of older workers in our society.
A program undertaken by the national employment service advisory group in Toronto, which has been widely quoted and is quoted by the international labour office, showed that by interviewing older workers not only were some opportunities found for these

workers but the self-respect of the workers was built up and many went out and got jobs themselves, when prior to that they were depressed by the social mores which condemned them to the industrial heap.
With regard to this problem we have to change our attitude; we have to change the attitude not only of industry, not only of employers but we have to change the attitude of our society. We are providing benefits for older people and for younger people, and we must not assume that we are the only social welfare society that the world has ever seen. Our particular problem is an aspect of industrial society; it is an aspect of the decline of patriarchal society. Patriarchal society looked after older people; rural society absorbed to some extent older people. We live in a largely individualistic and industrial society and the welfare state is our answer to that hiatus which has been created in our society by the growth of this highly individualized and industrialized economy. We have to change our attitudes; we must carry on a large program of education, and we must show to employers the great waste consequent in the attitudes they have towards the employment of older workers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to the motion just moved, that the subject matter of this bill be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations I am assuming I am in order if I discuss the subject matter of the bill. The purpose of the bill is to add to the act now on the statute books a provision that extends the field of discrimination against which we are trying to guard in our employment practices. It would ensure that age is not used in a purely prejudicial manner against a prospective employee.
The act now on the statute books which this bill seeks to amend ensures that certain factors cannot be used as a means of barring employment. It ensures that prejudice and bigotry will not prevent people from getting a job and it specifically enumerates the factors of race, national origin, colour or religion.
I do not think there is any question in anybody's mind that these factors already in the act have any bearing on a person's capability in carrying out an employment function. I do not think that any member of the house feels that race, national origin, colour or religion matter in terms of a person's ability to carry out his function. The amendment would add age to these factors.
To my mind the factor of age is one of several grey areas. I am very much against, as we all are, prejudice on the ground of any of the factors already listed; but what about linguistic ability? What about a provision that would state that an employer cannot discriminate because of somebody's ability to speak a certain language? You might have a situation where a person of foreign birth is applying for a job and has a very heavy accent. The prospective employer might, because he had a prejudice against people of that person's racial background, discriminate
2574	HOUSE OF
Canada Fair Employment Practices Act against him and because of his linguistic ability say: I will not take you.
On the other hand, there may be quite valid reasons for not employing a person with a very heavy accent. He might be applying for the type of job where his communicative ability was a key factor, in which case the employer would be justified in disqualifying this person for employment. This to me is a grey area. How do you know? It is very difficult to decide whether or not in the case I have just outlined the person is being discriminated against because of his linguistic ability or because of prejudice in the mind of the prospective employer.

If the hon. member will be patient, I was trying to indicate that there are certain categories of discrimination now in the act which are very clearcut, and that there are others where there can be some doubt; but I am coming now to the one specifically mentioned in the bill before us, age. I wanted to indicate that age also is one of those factors that can sometimes matter and at other times does not matter in terms of a person's ability to carry out a job. There are times when, for obvious reasons, the age of the person is important. There are times when it does not matter. There are several examples.
Some years ago when I was establishing a business I engaged a person for a function that normally would be a function that a young person would perform. It involved physical activity out of doors in all sorts of weather. I did not take a young man; I took an older man. This person has been with me for a number of years and has carried out the work extremely well. In the normal course of events one would have thought I would have been quite justified in saying to this person: No, you are too old for this job. It is very difficult indeed to tell.
At the same time I engaged this man I employed another man. His type of work was different and I hired a very young man, a man who according to the normal rules of
CMr. Hahn.]

the game might not have had enough experience. I could have discriminated against him by saying: You are too young-but I did not. It is very difficult in these cases to draw hard and fast rules. How do you know specifically whether age is or is not a factor in regard to a person's capability to carry out a job? It is extremely difficult to define.
There is a third kind of grey area of this type. A company may want to engage a person for a function for which age does not matter, but let us assume for a moment they want to engage a man to act as understudy to a senior person already in the organization. The age of the understudy does not matter in terms of his ability to carry out the job; but in terms of the long term development plans of the company age is a factor, if the company is looking forward to providing a replacement against the retirement of the more senior person. Is that company discriminating or not discriminating if they say that they would like a younger man for this particular function?
It seems to me that the major problem we face in this proposed legislation is that we are going to set out an area of discrimination and are going to say that an employer cannot discriminate against somebody because of age, and unless age is a bona fide occupational qualification he should disregard it in his hiring practices. It is exceedingly difficult, if not almost impossible at times, to determine whether age is a bona fide occupational qualification, because a person's capability to carry out the work is not the only factor. I think we must assume that the organization doing the hiring must have some plans for the future and must be able to carry out those plans, and if this involves selecting people in a certain age bracket the company should be allowed to do so.
This is not to say that I support, condone or agree with rank discrimination on the ground of age, because I feel that to discriminate only because of age, to turn a man down only because of age, is wrong. I should like to try to find an answer to the problem but I do not think this legislation is the right answer. I am afraid it could lead to all sorts of litigation. Indeed, if the bill is put on the statute books and is to mean anything it must lead to all sorts of litigation, and I think there would be great difficulty in establishing objective yardsticks to use. So I think we would wind up with an enactment on the statute books that would be unworkable. I do not think that this is the sort of thing we should do in this parliament. I think we

should be very careful to try to put on the statute books acts that will work.
What is the answer to this problem of the older worker? As the hon. member for York South (Mr. Gelber) pointed out, and as I heartily agree, in many respects the older workers are superior workers. There are prejudices in the minds of many people against hiring older people. The approach suggested by the hon. member for York South appears to me a much more logical approach, that is to try a fundamental educational program on the employers. This, in my opinion, would produce far better results than putting unworkable legislation on the statute books. I believe that if this bill is passed it is not going to solve the problem. Again, without going through all the ramifications of the problem, I think the hon. member for York South covered a number of the reasons why older people have difficulty in getting jobs.
This particular measure does not answer many of these problems. On the other hand, it is going to create problems in terms of litigation. I think it will create problems on the one hand without, on the other hand, achieving the objective we seek to achieve. I feel it will, in fact, do more harm than good. I certainly hope this bill is referred to the committee on industrial relations for study this afternoon. If the committee ascertains it is not possible to enforce or administer this type

Yes, I spoke on the main motion, but we are considering the amendment now.
This civilian employee of the Department of National Defence received a communication from the civilian personnel officer advising him of a recommendation for his release due to age. Those words were used in a letter which had been forwarded by the higher authorities. I put a question on the order paper which will be found on page 2195 of Hansard for April 15, 1964. It is question No. 640, and reads as follows:
Are civilian employees of the Department of National Defence dismissed from employment on the grounds of age before reaching 65 years?
The answer by the associate minister reads as follows:
The normal retiring age for civilian employees of the Department of National Defence is 65. There is provision in the Public Service Superannuation Act and regulations whereby a deputy head, with the concurrence of the civil service commission, may at any time, for reason only of age, terminate the employment of a contributor who has attained 60 years of age. It is the policy of the Department of National Defence to retire persons between age 60 and 65 years, by reason of age, only in unusual cases where continued employment involves a serious problem.
The answer is not completely clear, but it does admit that whereas the normal retiring age is 65, the department does retire people at an earlier age, on the grounds of age, and that is precisely the case which has been drawn to my attention, the release of an employee "due to age". To have the subject matter of this bill considered by a committee would throw some light on the policy of the government with regard to the problem of employment, and the release from employment, of people by reason of age.
I would think a committee would want to investigate very thoroughly this particular question, and see what the grounds are on


which government departments release people simply on the grounds of age when it is normal, as the answer to my question indicated, to continue people until-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF AGE
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Does he realize that the clause in the Civil Service Act, referred to in the answer he has just read, was put in that act by the government of which he was a member?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT DISCRIMINATION BECAUSE OF AGE
speechtext:
Well, that is irrelevant. If it is a bad provision I don't care what government put it in; I would say throw it out. This has not come to my attention before, and if our government made a mistake we are quite prepared to admit it. The present government spends all its time apologizing for the mistakes it is making.
My point is that in this period, when we have become more sympathetic towards the question of employment and the age factor, when we have been attempting to deal with the employment of people over the age of 45 years, when we have been attempting to continue employment throughout the sixties-and in various circumstances suggesting that people should carry on until they are 70-surely we must look at any rules, regulations or provisions within the government service which permit retirement before the age of 65, simply on the grounds of age and, if there are arbitrary decisions being made, then some modification of these provisions should be entered into.
The reason I support the proposal that the subject matter be referred to a committee is that it is impossible under these circumstances to discuss the subject fully or to get the necessary answers that one would require. Whereas, a committee of the house is admirably suited to get the information, to have witnesses brought before it, to have the officials summoned, to study the matter and clear it up by suggesting modifications to some of our statutes or to the regulations of the civil service commission, modifications which would bring to an end the release of people from employment simply on the grounds of age.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak only a short while. First I would like to say I think the subject matter of the bill is worthy of close examination and should be placed before a committee for study, but the other thing I would like to say is that I doubt the practicability of the bill itself. I think it one of those cases where we sort of give lip service to something,

and there are so many loopholes that nobody can catch up with one who is actually transgressing in the situation.
One of the things that has caused this legislation to appear on the books has been the fact that pensions have been the criterion so far as hiring older people is concerned. The fact that people are getting on towards the pension age has worked against their securing employment; but now, if we get a universal pension plan with portability, this will have a great effect on the chances of the older workers becoming employed.
I look forward to our getting a pension plan suitable for all Canadians, with the portability that will make it possible for the individual who finds himself out of employment to take his pension with him, so that his prospective new employer will not look askance at him because of the pension situation.

Mr. Speaker, if I may revert for a moment to the few remarks made by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt)-by the way they were not nearly as good as the cheese his country produces-he did say one thing about which I should like to comment. He drew attention to the fact that the government, through the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mac-Eachen), introduced a measure to encourage industry to employ persons over 45 years of age who had been unemployed for six of the previous nine months.
While, as he said, this measure has not been taken up by employers on as wide a scale as we would have hoped, nevertheless it has provided a very substantial financial incentive for them to employ older workers. To my knowledge this is the first effort on the part of any government to set an example by actual legislation to encourage industry to employ older workers.
The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe) has just pointed out that we are now hoping to have a comprehensive, portable pension plan, again devised by this government, and this too will provide an enormous incentive to the employment of older workers. Indeed, as I was sitting here listening to some of the speeches, particularly from the official opposition, I could not help recalling that these two measures this government has taken have been by far the most substantial strides ever taken to encourage the employment of persons who are getting on in years and who have such great difficulty getting jobs.
When this matter was debated three years ago, to be exact on May 5, 1961, speaker after
24, 1964	2577
Canada Fair Employment Practices Act speaker on the opposite side got up and talked about it. Presumably the government of the day spent a good deal of time talking about it, just as it spent a good deal of time talking about how wonderful it would be to have a portable, national, contributory pension scheme; but nothing was done about it. Neither was anything done on the score of encouraging industry to employ older workers, or getting the kind of pension scheme going that would make for the encouragement of the employment of older workers.
Therefore since this government has, in a very short time, taken these two steps which were talked about since 1961, and earlier, by the previous government, and since it is quite clear that the matter of the older worker is one that has been of very great concern to this government, in particular to the Minister of Labour, and in the case of the pension plan to the other ministers as well, we can pretty well rely on the interest and concern on this side of the house in this problem, an interest and concern which are sufficient to make us want to do something about it.
I see that the bill which it is proposed to amend, the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, contains no provision for preventing discrimination on the ground of sex which, it seems to me, is an extraordinary omission and I hope the hon. member will-

speechtext: You look after the sex and I look after the age.

If I were the hon. member, I would not like that at all. Perhaps we could be offered an amendment which would prevent discrimination against women workers, because such discrimination is widespread in many places.
What puzzles me about the amendment is the phrase "unless age is a bona fide occupational qualification". I have found it difficult to understand what this really means and how it would be interpreted. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather) in his speech on April 3 really did not tell us what that means and I feel there is a danger it would mean all things to all men. If an employer were to say: "I am sorry, but this particular job is one which requires people under the age of 45", his word would be taken, there being no arbitrary way of judging whether the job was, indeed, one which could be done only by people in certain age groups.
This is a particular weakness. If we are to include this reference to age it would seem to me better to do so without making any qualification at all, except of course that obviously one would not include child labour.

Canada Fair Employment Practices Act It is interesting that we should have spent so many years in this country in the past fighting to get some degree of age discrimination, namely to prevent child labour, only to discover that there is discrimination at the other end against older workers.
The bill should be examined very closely before an age factor is introduced into the act. I agree that the act is not complete. As I have indicated, there is no clause in it to help women, and there is nothing about age in it at the moment. But the government it seems to me is already seized with this problem, as indeed is the other place right now. The interest being taken in it is greater than for a number of years. The government has already taken two important steps to encourage the employment of older workers, and undoubtedly further steps will be taken, steps which I suggest will be in the end more effective than the clauses which the hon. member wishes to introduce into the act.
For my part I am prepared to see a continuation of the progress we have made in this field over the past several months. I am not sure that the industrial relations standing committee would have much further to contribute on this subject. I believe additional progress can be made by other means. I was interested to notice that in one branch of the government service, the Canadian penitentiaries service, an attempt has been made recently to employ older workers in occupations other than those of guards.
